title: Effect of a virtual home hospital pathway on length of stay and recurrent presentations in septic stone patients
text:

                                                        on length of stay and recurrent presentations in
                                                        septic stone patients
                                                        Matthew Mancuso, Sabrina Pattar, Patrick Albers, Michael Jacka, Nathan Hoy


INTRODUCTION
- In a publicly funded healthcare system,
  resource allocation is crucial
- Patients with septic stones (SS) remain
  hospitalized until (1) clinically stable and (2)
  culture-directed oral antibiotic therapy can be
  initiated
- This typically leads to a prolonged hospital
  stay after source control
- We introduced a novel Virtual Home Hospital
  (VHH) pathway to enable early discharge with
  outpatient physician monitoring, including lab
  work and home-based IV antibiotics pending
  rationalization
                                                     RESULTS
- Our primary objective was to assess for length     - There were no significant differences in age (p=0.93) or gender (p=0.45) between groups

  included re-presentation rates, and other            nephrostomy tubes (p=0.20)
  complications                                      - 17 (17%) non-VHH patients required ICU admission, while only 1 (3%) VHH patient did (p=0.03)
                                                     - LOS was significantly longer in the non-VHH compared to the VHH groups; 3.8±3 days vs 2.3±2.3days respectively (p=0.005)
                                                     - Antibiotic duration was longer in the non-VHH group at 12.3±2.8 days compared to 10.2±3.1 days for the VHH group (p=<0.001)
                                                     - No significant differences were observed for emergency or clinic re-presentations (p=0.77, p=0.06)

title: Global Prostate Research Disparities: A 25-Year Bibliometric Analysis of Authorship Equity and Disease Focus
text:

                                     A 25-Year Bibliometric Analysis of Benign and Malignant Disease
                                                          3                   1             2            3                  3

INTRODUCTION                                               RESULTS
•   Equitable research representation is essential         • 89,406 publications from 160 countries were included.
    for globally relevant prostate disease                 • HICs produced 78.8% of authorship and 78.0% of corresponding
    knowledge and clinical practice.                         authorship, whereas LICs contributed 0.09% and 0.11%.
•   Despite growth in prostate research, major             • International collaborations accounted for 16.6% of publications, yet
    disparities in authorship contribution persist           87.9% were driven by HIC authors, with LIC involvement only 0.22%.
    across country income groups.
                                                           • From 2000 to 2024, HIC representation decreased from 96.6% to
•   We performed a 25-year bibliometric analysis to          66.9%, with significant increases in UMIC and LMIC participation.
    evaluate global disparities in prostate research
    by income group and disease focus.                     • Malignant prostate research dominated the literature (79.9%)
                                                             compared with benign disease (14.2%).
METHODS
• Bibliometric analysis of Scopus-indexed prostate
  publications from 2000–2025, searched on May
  27, 2025.
• Metadata were extracted; affiliations were
  assigned to World Bank income groups, and
  publications were classified as benign or
  malignant.
• Inequality and temporal trends were assessed
  using Lorenz curves, Gini coefficients, Mann–
  Kendall testing, and chi-square analysis.                                                                                                 CONCLUSIONS
                                                                                                                                            •   Despite increased global participation, prostate
                                                                                                                                                research remains dominated by high-income countries.
                                                                                                                                            •   The literature remains heavily focused on malignant
                                                                                                                                                disease, with benign research comparatively
                                                                                                                                                underrepresented.
                                                                                                                                            •   Strengthening collaboration in LMICs and LICs is
                                                                                                                                                essential to advance more equitable global scientific
                                                                                                                                                progress.

 The De Ritis ratio, defined as the serum aspartate aminotransferase to alanine aminotransferase ratio, has been reported as a prognostic biomarker in various malignancies, reflecting tumor metabolic activity
 and systemic inflammation.
   Despite its growing relevance in oncology, the prognostic significance of the De Ritis ratio in patients with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC) receiving upfront therapy remains poorly
   understood.

Methods
   This multicenter retrospective study included 1,204 patients with mHSPC who received upfront therapy between December 2015 and September 2025.
   The treatment regimens consisted of docetaxel, androgen receptor signaling inhibitors, or a combination of docetaxel and darolutamide.
   The De Ritis ratio was measured at the time of mHSPC diagnosis. The optimal cut-off value for predicting progression to castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) was determined using receiver operating
   characteristic curve analysis. Patients were stratified into two groups based on the De Ritis ratio: lower and higher.
   Multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression analyses were performed to evaluate the impact of a higher De Ritis ratio on CRPC-free survival and overall survival (OS).

Results
   The median age and follow-up duration were 70 years and 55 months, respectively.
   The median De Ritis ratio was 1.3, and the optimal cut-off value was determined to be 1.8. Among the 1,204 patients, 231 (19%) had a De Ritis ratio above the cut-off (Fig. 1).
   Although the rate of PSA decline ≥90% was lower in the higher De Ritis ratio group, the difference was not statistically significant (Fig. 2).
   In contrast, the rate of PSA decline ≥99% was significantly lower in the higher ratio group compared to the lower ratio group (Fig. 3).
   Both CRPC-free survival (Fig. 4) and OS (Fig. 5) were significantly shorter in the higher De Ritis ratio group.
   After adjusting for age, performance status, Gleason score ≥8, CHHATED high-volume disease, initial PSA level, hemoglobin <12g/dL, and LDH ≥326 U/L, a higher De Ritis ratio remained independently
   associated with shorter CRPC-free survival and OS (Fig. 6).

  However, due to the limited sample size, definitive conclusions could not be drawn. Therefore, the present study aimed to externally validate this risk model in a larger, independent cohort.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       Months

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   Sci Rep. 2025;15:10814.

Methods
  This multicenter retrospective study included 794 patients with mCRPC who received Ra-223 treatment.
  First, multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression analysis was performed to assess the association between OS from Ra-223 initiation and the three previously identified risk factors: EOD >1, incomplete
  Ra-223 treatment (<6 cycles), and PSA >10 ng/mL at the start of Ra-223.
  Patients were then stratified based on the number of these risk factors. OS was estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method and compared across groups using the log-rank test.
  Furthermore, the predictive performance of these factors for 2-year and 3-year OS was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis.

Results
  The median age at Ra-223 initiation was 75 years. The median follow-up durations from CRPC diagnosis and Ra-223 initiation were 36 and 16 months, respectively.
  In multivariable analysis adjusted for age, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status ≥1, Gleason score ≥8, prior lines of mCRPC treatment, and time from CRPC diagnosis to Ra-223 initiation,
  all three risk factors were significantly associated with shorter OS (Fig. 2).
  Kaplan–Meier curves demonstrated clear separation according to the number of risk factors (Fig. 3).
  Patients with two or three risk factors had significantly shorter OS from both Ra-223 initiation and CRPC diagnosis compared to those with zero or one risk factor (Fig. 4 and 5).
  The area under the ROC curve (AUC) for predicting 2-year and 3-year OS was 0.811 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.781–0.841) and 0.778 (95% CI: 0.745–0.811), respectively (Fig. 6)

Conclusion
   This external validation confirmed that EOD >1, PSA >10 ng/mL at Ra-223 initiation, and incomplete Ra-223 treatment
   are independent prognostic factors for poor OS in patients with mCRPC.

       INTRODUCTION


  Impostor Syndrome (IS) and perfectionism contribute to psychological distress among physicians in training.
  IS involves persistent self-doubt despite objective competence, while Perfectionism is characterized by
  excessive self-criticism and unrealistic standards.

  Data in urology residents, particularly in Latin America, are limited.




                                                                                                                                                          AIM


      This study evaluated the prevalence of IS and perfectonism and rheir association among urology residents in Mexico.




                                                                               METHODS


      An annonymus online questionnare was administered to 404 participants.
      IS was assessed using the Clance Impostor Phenomen Scale (CIPS).

      Perfectionism was assessed with the Frost Multidimensional Perfectionism scale (FMPS).

      Descriptive statistics and Spearman correlation were used to analyze associations

INTRODUCTION                                                                                                                         RESULTS
Fournier’s gangrene is a rare but life-threatening necrotizing
fasciitis of the perineal, genital, and perianal regions. While
acute mortality and surgical management are well described,
evidence on long-term morbidity after survival remains scarce.
Extensive      tissue  destruction,    repeated    debridement,
reconstructive procedures, and the genital localization of the
disease may result in sustained impairment of urinary, bowel,
sexual, psychosocial, and quality-of-life outcomes.
Objective: To systematically assess long-term mortality,
functional outcomes, and quality of life among patients who
survived Fournier’s gangrene.




METHODS
A systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA
guidance and the Cochrane Handbook and was prospectively
registered in PROSPERO.

Structured survivorship
Because of substantial heterogeneity in follow-up duration and                                                                                                                                                                        care and prospective studies using standardized, validated follow-up
outcome reporting, no quantitative pooling was performed.                                                                                                                                                                             instruments are needed to better define long-term recovery, guide

 1. Low  sensitivity of DNA detection rate in urine                                       The upper urinary tract hosts diverse environmental bacteria, while the

                                                                                            The upper urinary tract was characterized by a higher prevalence of environmental and
                                                                                          biofilm-forming bacteria, including Shigella flexneri/Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus
                                                                                          epidermidis, and Staphylococcus lugdunensis. These organisms are known for their ability to
                                                                                          adhere to surfaces and form biofilms, which may contribute to persistent colonization and stone
                                                                                          formation. In contrast, the lower urinary tract was predominantly enriched with typical
                                                                                          commensal species, reflecting a more stable and homeostatic microbial environment.

3.                                                                                          In a subset of five patients in which comparisons were made between stone-bearing and non-
   and renal pelvis reveals site-dependent community
   shifts                                                                                 stone-bearing sides, the dominant taxa varied considerably across samples, and no consistent
                                                                                          pattern of microbial enrichment was observed. However, it is important to note that low detection
                                                                                          rates, particularly in low-biomass samples, may have introduced bias, preferentially highlighting
                                                                                          taxa present in higher quantities and potentially underestimating the true diversity in the urinary
                                                                                          microbiome.

                                                                                                                                     Conclusion:
                                                                                            These preliminary findings highlight the presence of bacterial taxa in both bladder and renal
                                                                                          pelvic urine, suggesting that distinct patients may harbor different microbial profiles and
                                                                                          bacterial species potentially associated with stone formation, which may facilitate crystal
                                                                                          nucleation and aggregation through biofilm-mediated mechanisms. Thus, understanding the
                                                                                          interplay between bacterial biofilms and calcium-based urinary stones warrants further
                                                                                          investigations.

   INTRODUCTION                                                                                        Authors                   RESULTS
   Leonard Paul Wershub (1901-1969) was a New York City urologist and                                                            Dr. Wershub was a urologist at New York Medical College from 1925 until his death. The archivist at NYMC was enormously
   urohistorian. He chose to work at a homeopathic hospital and medical                                                          helpful in tracking down personal materials on him and his urologic practice. Dr. Wershub wrote five major textbooks, yet
   school, and had a long and successful academic/clinical career at New                                                         never rose to national prominence, possibly because of his clinical location.
   York Medical College (NYMC).
                                                                                                                                 •  Wershub married Miriam, and they had one son, Stuart, who sadly died in 2020
   • Born in NYC on May 5, 1901                                                                                                  •  He practiced in NYC his entire life and was Consulting Editor for The Chironian, NYMC’s monthly magazine
   • Student at DeWitt Clinton High School                                                                                       •  He wrote his own section in The Chironian, wrote other articles on urology, and maintained a urologic practice
   • Attended Yale University in 1919                                                                                            •  He was fully academic and published five books in his lifetime
   • Then attended Columbia College                                                                                              •  He was intensely interested in NYMC and became involved in NYC medical politics
   • Earned his MD from NYMC in 1927                                                                                             •  Attached in the supplemental images is a solo review of Wershub’s magnum opus
   • Residency at Beth Israel Hospital, 1927–1929                                                                                •  Sadly, there is no eulogy for Dr. Wershub and little fanfare over his historical labors
   • Joined NYMC faculty in 1930 and never left                                                                                  •  There was, however, one excellent review of his textbook on the history of urology in England
   • Became curator of the NYMC museum                                                                                           •  He never appears to have been bothered by his lack of notoriety
   • Was interested in the history of medicine and                                                                               •  Wershub published his little-regarded and often ignored textbook of urologic history in 1970

   •   Minimal writing exists on Wershub or his urologic history work                                                            Wershub’s historical contribution was the first full U.S. textbook history of urology entitled Urology: From Antiquity to the 20th
   •   We sought his textbook, Urology: From Antiquity to the 20th Century                                                       Century, published in 1970, two years prior to the more heralded Leonard Murphy work. His magnum opus remains unique in
   •   Next, we placed his work in context with Murphy and Herman                                                                its layout, scope, and scholarship. His contributions to the history of urology were titanic and very much underappreciated.

                                  INTRODUCTION
Women with bladder cancer (BC) frequently experience pelvic floor disorders (PFDs) that persist
throughout diagnosis, treatment, and survivorship. These symptoms, including urinary incontinence,
voiding dysfunction, pelvic pain, and sexual dysfunction, can substantially affect quality of life but are not
routinely screened or addressed in clinical practice. Treatment-related factors such as intravesical therapy
and radical cystectomy may further worsen pelvic floor symptoms, while gaps in counseling and
survivorship care limit access to effective interventions. The Survivorship and Pelvic floor InterventioNs
(SPIN) program was designed to integrate systematic PFD screening and urogynecologic care into bladder
cancer management.


                                                 AIMS

    urogynecologic program.                                                                                           Table 1: Characteristics of the SPIN Cohort                               Figure 1: Patient-Reported Outcomes at 3-Month Follow-Up

                                          METHODS

                                                                                                                 36 women with bladder cancer were enrolled in the SPIN study (median age 70 years; 94.2% White, 51.4%

title: Impact of chronic kidney disease on prognosis in patients with high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer who underwent adjuvant bacillus Calmette-Guérin therapy
text:
Impact of chronic kidney disease on prognosis in patients with high-risk non-muscle-
invasive bladder cancer who underwent adjuvant bacillus Calmette-Guérin therapy
 N. Fujita1, T. Narita1, M. Momota1, H. Ito2, K. Yoshikawa3, and S. Hatakeyama1                                *Corresponding author’s E-mail address: naonao707012@hirosaki-u.ac.jp
                                                                                                                                                                                                         IP02-18
 Department of Urology, 1) Hirosaki University Graduate School of Medicine, Hirosaki, Japan; 2) Aomori Rosai Hospital, Hachinohe, Japan 3) Aomori City Hospital, Aomori, Japan

Background
  Immune dysfunction is a well-recognized complication in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), potentially impairing host defense mechanisms against malignancy.
  Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) therapy is a cornerstone of adjuvant treatment for high-risk non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC), relying on robust local immune activation to prevent tumor recurrence
  and progression. However, the efficacy of BCG may be compromised in individuals with CKD due to impaired immunological responses.
  We hypothesized that patients with CKD may exhibit suboptimal antitumor immunity following adjuvant BCG therapy, resulting in inferior oncological outcomes.
Methods
 We conducted a multi-institutional retrospective study assessing 209 patients with high-risk NMIBC who underwent transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) and subsequent adjuvant induction BCG
 therapy from December 1998 to April 2019.
  Patients were divided into two groups: those with preoperative estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) ≥60 mL/min/1.73 m2 (non-CKD group), and those with eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2 (CKD group).
  Multivariable analyses were performed to assess the impact of CKD on intravesical recurrence and muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC) progression, adjusting for the competing risk of death using the Fine-
  Gray competing risk regression model.
Results
  Median age and follow-up period after TURBT were 72 years and 45 months, respectively. Of 209 patients, 71 (34%) were diagnosed with CKD before TURBT.
  In the Fine-Gray competing risk regression model, CKD showed significantly higher probabilities of intravesical recurrence and MIBC progression, with an adjusted subdistribution hazard ratio of 1.886 (95%
  confidence interval [CI] 1.069–3.330, P = 0.028) and 3.740 (95% CI 1.060–13.20, P = 0.040), respectively (Fig. C and D).
  Moreover, metastasis-free survival,cancer-specific survival, and overall survival in the CKD group were significantly shorter than those in thenon-CKD group (Fig. E-G).

title: Prognostic significance of symptom-driven recurrence in high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer
text:
Prognostic significance of symptom-driven recurrence in high-risk non-muscle-invasive
bladder cancer
N. Fujita1, M. Momota1, H. Ito2, K. Yoshikawa3, and S. Hatakeyama1                               *Corresponding author’s E-mail address: naonao707012@hirosaki-u.ac.jp                                         IP02-19
Department of Urology, 1) Hirosaki University Graduate School of Medicine, Hirosaki, Japan; 2) Aomori Rosai Hospital, Hachinohe, Japan 3) Aomori City Hospital, Aomori, Japan
Background
  Because patients with high-risk non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) have high recurrence and progression rates, it is recommended that they undergo intensive surveillance after transurethral
  resection of bladder tumor (TURBT).
  However, no study has demonstrated that such an intensive surveillance contributes to improving oncological outcomes. Moreover, no study has investigated an association between symptomatic recurrence
  and poor prognosis in patients with high-risk NMIBC.
Methods
 We retrospectively evaluated 428 patients with primary high-risk NMIBC who underwent TURBT from November 1993 to April 2019.
  Of the 428 patients, 140 had experienced recurrence at any site and were divided into two groups: patients who had experienced recurrence detected by the surveillance (asymptomatic group) and patients
  who experienced recurrence detected by a symptom-driven investigation (symptomatic group).
  Background-adjusted multivariable analyses with the inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) method were performed to evaluate the impact of symptomatic recurrence on cancer-specific survival
  (CSS) and overall survival (OS) after first recurrence in patients who experienced recurrence.
  Moreover, multivariable analysis was performed to identify predictive factors of symptomatic recurrence in the entire cohort
Results
  Median age and follow-up periods were 72 years and 55 months, respectively. Of the 140 patients who experienced recurrence, 34 (24%) were diagnosed by a symptom-driven investigation (symptomatic
  group).
  Muscle invasive bladder cancer progression rate at the time of first recurrence in the symptomatic group was significantly higher than that in the asymptomatic group (Fig. 4).
  CSS and OS after the first recurrence in the symptomatic group were significantly shorter than those in the asymptomatic group (Fig. 5 and 6). In the background-adjusted multivariable analyses with the IPTW
  model, symptomatic recurrence was significantly associated with shorter CSS along with shorter OS after the first recurrence (Fig. 7).
  In the multivariable analysis, only tumor grade was selected as a significant predictive factor of symptomatic recurrence after TURBT (Table).

title: Early Apical Release in Holmium Laser Enucleation of the Prostate. Is It Worth it? A Meta-Analysis and Meta-Regression on Perioperative and Postoperative Outcomes.
text:
Early Apical Release in Holmium Laser Enucleation of the
                                                                    Prostate. Is It Worth It? A Meta-Analysis and Meta-Regression
                                                                    on Perioperative and Postoperative Outcomes

                                                                    Andrade M.A., Baldissera-Cardoso R., Amaral D.O., Cruz J.A.S., Paludo A.O., Weiss M., Berger M., Berger A.K., Miller N.




                                         PURPOSE
Holmium Laser Enucleation of the Prostate (HoLEP) is a well-established treatment for benign
prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), but early postoperative urinary incontinence remains a concern. The
Early Apical Release (EAR) technique aims to reduce sphincteric strain through early apical
mucosa mobilization. However, evidence supporting its superiority is limited and inconsistent. This
meta-analysis evaluates the efficacy and safety of EAR versus standard HoLEP techniques,
focusing on perioperative parameters, complications, and continence outcomes.

                                         METHODS
PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane were systematically searched through April 2025, following
PRISMA guidelines. Outcomes assessed: operative time, AUASS at 3 months, Clavien-Dindo
complications (≤2 and ≥3), overall complications, and incontinence (<30 days and 1–3 months). A
random-effects model was used; meta-regression explored moderators of heterogeneity.



                                          RESULTS
Six studies including 3,538 patients (1,440 EAR, 2,098 standard) were analyzed. No significant
differences were observed in AUASS at 3 months (MD -0.10; 95% CI -1.42 to 1.22; p=0.88) or
operative time (MD -0.09 min; 95% CI -11.51 to 11.33; p=0.99). Early postoperative incontinence
did not differ between groups: <30 days (OR 0.33; 95% CI 0.10–1.03; p=0.06) and 1–3 months                Figure 1 - PRISMA flow diagram of study screening and selection.
(OR 0.38; 95% CI 0.13–1.14; p=0.09). EAR was associated with significantly higher complication
rates: Clavien-Dindo ≤2 (OR 1.44; p=0.006), ≥3 (OR 2.53; p=0.01), and overall (OR 1.46;
p=0.0004). Meta-regression revealed that prostate size (β=-0.0891, p=0.015) and incontinence
definition (β=-3.2059, p=0.001) significantly moderated the effect on incontinence risk.




                                      CONCLUSION
EAR was not superior to standard HoLEP techniques in reducing postoperative incontinence,
with no differences observed in symptom relief or operative time. Importantly, EAR was
associated with a significantly higher overall complication rate, including both Clavien-Dindo
grade ≤2 and ≥3 complications. While the choice of surgical approach often reflects personal
preference and expertise, urologists should be aware of the potentially higher complication rates         Figure 2 - Forest plots: (A) AUASS at 3 months; (B) operative time; (C) postoperative incontinence (<30
associated with EAR. Familiarity with both techniques may be advantageous to optimize patient             days and 1–3 months); (D) Clavien-Dindo ≤2, ≥3, and overall complications.
outcomes and tailor the surgical approach to individual clinical scenarios.

    SCREENING WITH PSA ≥1.0ng/mL + AI-ASSISTED MRI PROVIDES THE OPTIMAL BALANCE BETWEEN CANCER
                                    DETECTION AND HARM REDUCTION

INTRODUCTION                                                                    P1: UPFRONT MRI                                       P2: PSA ≥1 THEN MRI                                      P3: PSA ≥3 THEN MRI
Prostate cancer screening with PSA leads to unnecessary
biopsies and overdiagnosis
The IP1-PROSTAGRAM study showed that upfront MRI
could reduce these harms
We evaluated an artificial intelligence decision support (AI-
DSS) tool to further reduce harms



METHODS
IP1-PROSTAGRAM was a prospective screening study in
which men aged 50-69 underwent PSA and non-contrast
abbreviated MRI (~15 minutes)

The Pi™ AI-DSS was retrospectively applied to the IP1-
PROSTAGRAM dataset (n= 371)

The AI-DSS integrates an MRI-AI risk score, radiologist PI-
RADS score, and PSA density to produce a risk score to
guide biopsy

We compared three patient selection pathways:

• P1: Upfront MRI for all participants
• P2: PSA ≥1.0ng/mL then MRI
• P3: PSA ≥3.0ng/mL then MRI

For each pathway, biopsy was recommended for:

• PI-RADS ≥3
• PI-RADS ≥4
• AI-DSS risk score

We compared biopsy rates and outcomes across the
                                                                          CONCLUSIONS
                                                                          PSA triage using a threshold of ≥1.0 ng/mL, followed by MRI with AI-DSS offers the optimal benefit-harm ratio

title: Towards Clinical Translation of a Real-time, Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Assisted Cystoscopy System for Bladder Cancer Detection
text:
IP04-26: Towards Clinical Translation of a Real-time, Artificial Intelligence (AI)
                                   Assisted Cystoscopy System for Bladder Cancer Detection
                                                1           1           1               1                 1
                                   Calvin C Zhao , Max Siauw , Liang Qiu , Timothy J Lee , Kathleen E Mach , Joseph C Liao 1
                                   1Department of Urology, Stanford University School of Medicine




                                     Introduction                                                                                                                       Visualization Modes:
White light cystoscopy is the cornerstone of bladder cancer detection and surveillance;
however, challenges remain, including identification of carcinoma in situ, multifocal tumors,
and distinguishing cancerous and benign lesions. Computer-vision artificial intelligence (AI)
models for tumor detection have strong potential to overcome these limitations. This study
aims to address the clinical translation hurdles related to workflow compatibility and usability
by integrating an AI-assisted cystoscopy system in clinical settings.
                                                                                                                                                                        Centroid               Box
                                        Methods
We developed an end-to-end AI-assisted cystoscopy system featuring a
compact, custom-built video processing hub and an intuitive graphical user
interface for integration with standard endoscopy towers. The hub supports
up to four HDMI connections, enabling real-time switching between various
video inputs via a front-panel control. Equipped with an NVIDIA RTX 5060
graphics card, the system provides real-time AI inference displayed as                                                                                                  Outline             Heatmap
toggleable, low-latency overlays. A foot pedal allows the operator
to quickly cycle through or deactivate AI overlays. For procedural
safety, a hardware bypass button ensures the primary video feed
remains uninterrupted in the event of a system error. A structured
survey was designed to assess clinician user experience, focusing                                                                                 Results
on interface usability and utility.
                                                                                                   The platform was successfully deployed in 5 operating room and 6 clinic cystoscopy procedures. Survey
                                                                                                   feedback from 8 physician users confirmed the system was user-friendly and minimally disruptive to
                                                                                                   workflow. Reported limitations include noticeable system latency during transurethral resection and
                                                                                                   false positive detections of non-cancerous lesions, such as resection beds.

BACKGROUND: Alport Syndrome (AS) is a hereditary form of chronic kidney disease characterized by progressive damage to the glomerular filtration barrier (GFB), ultimately resulting in proteinuria and
kidney failure. Although GFB impairment is a hallmark of AS, the precise mechanisms driving glomerular endothelial cell (GEC) injury and the subsequent effects on tubular health are not well understood. To
address this, we employ a nephron-on-a-chip (NOAC) model to investigate the molecular pathways mediating glomerular-tubular crosstalk (Scheme 1). Our recent studies indicate that GEC injury occurs
prior to the onset of proteinuria and that GECs overproduce serpin A3, which contributes to proximal tubule damage and functional decline. This work aims to elucidate the role of serpin A3 in mediating both
glomerular and tubular dysfunction in AS.

title: Predictive value of hyaluronan for severe acute kidney injury development in urosepsis
text:
Predictive value of hyaluronan for severe acute kidney injury development in urosepsis
 N. Fujita1,*, Y. Tobisawa2, T. Yoneyama1, M. Momota1 , H. Horiguchi1, H. Ito3, K. Yoshikawa4, and S. Hatakeyama1
                                                                                                                                                                                                                             IP07-10
 Department of Urology, 1Hirosaki University Graduate School of Medicine, Hirosaki, Japan; 2Gifu University, Gifu, Japan; 3Aomori Rosai Hospital, Hachinohe, Japan; 4Aomori City Hospital, Aomori, Japan

 *Corresponding author’s E-mail address: naonao707012@hirosaki-u.ac.jp
Background
   Hyaluronan is a major glycosaminoglycan component of the endothelial glycocalyx, which coats the luminal surface of vascular endothelial cells (Fig. 1). It plays a pivotal role in
   maintaining vascular homeostasis by regulating thrombogenicity, modulating inflammatory responses, and preserving endothelial barrier integrity.
   Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a frequent and life-threatening complication in patients with urosepsis, yet the association between hyaluronan degradation and AKI development in this
   context remains poorly understood.
Methods                                                                                                                                                                                                                  KDIGO criteria
   This retrospective study included 145 patients with urosepsis who were treated between March 2017 and March 2019.
   AKI was defined according to the KDIGO criteria.
   Plasma hyaluronan levels were measured at admission using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay.
   Multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed to evaluate the association between glycocalyx injury and the development of severe AKI.
   Additionally, the predictive ability of elevated hyaluronan levels for severe AKI was assessed using receiver operating characteristic curve analysis and
   compared using net reclassification improvement (NRI) and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI).
Results                                                                                                                                                                         Univariable analyses for severe AKI development
   The median age of the cohort was 79 years. Of the 145 patients, 39 (27%) developed severe AKI (defined as KDIGO stage 2 or 3).
                                                                                                                                                                                                              Factor    P value   Odds ratio    95% CI
   Patients who developed severe AKI had significantly higher plasma hyaluronan levels than those who did not (Fig. 2).                                              Age                                   Continuous    0.047      1.03       1.00–1.07

   significantly associated with severe AKI development. In multivariable analysis, plasma hyaluronan level remained a significant                                   ECOG PS                               Continuous    0.257      1.13       0.91–1.41

BACKGROUND: Microplastics (MP), defined as synthetic polymer particles smaller than 5 millimeters, are increasingly recognized as environmental contaminants with potential health
consequences. Recent studies have identified MP in human tissues, including the kidney, raising concerns about their role in renal injury. Given the kidney’s central role in filtration and
waste elimination, this study aimed to evaluate the impact of MP exposure on renal cell function and structure, and to explore their potential contribution to kidney disease progression.

METHODS: Primary human renal cells (podocytes, glomerular endothelial cells (GEC), and proximal tubular cells (PTC)) were exposed to fluorescently labeled polystyrene MP (1 µm) in
vitro. MP uptake and cellular responses were assessed using live-cell imaging, flow cytometry, immunofluorescence, and protein array analysis. Functional effects were evaluated using
microfluidic organ-on-chip platforms that model glomerular and tubular compartments.

transport mechanisms, whereas glomerular endothelial cells (GEC) appear to permit passive diffusion (Fig. 3). Further inhibition
of specific endocytic pathways indicates that macropinocytosis is the predominant uptake mechanism in proximal tubular cells
(Fig. 4). Protein profiling revealed activation of oxidative stress and apoptosis pathways across different cell types (Fig.5).
Organ-on-chip studies using a glomerulus on a chip demonstrated compromised glomerular barrier integrity, evidenced by
increased albumin leakage (Fig.6).

title: Chronic Microplastic Exposure Alters Renal and Lower Urinary Tract Homeostasis in Healthy Mice
text:
CHRONIC MICROPLASTIC EXPOSURE ALTERS RENAL AND
                                                                            LOWER URINARY TRACT HOMEOSTASIS IN HEALTHY MICE
                                                                                       Velia Alcala 1, Mohammadreza Kasravi 1, Raquel Rodriguez1, Rachel Wen1, Laura Perin1, and Stefano Da Sacco1
                                                                                                                                        1Children’s Hospital Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA, USA




BACKGROUND: Microplastics (MP), synthetic particles <5 mm, are increasingly recognized as environmental contaminants with systemic health
implications. While their presence in human kidneys has been documented, the impact of chronic MP exposure on renal and lower urinary tract physiology
in healthy systems remains unclear. Given the kidney and bladder’s role in filtration and excretion, understanding MP biodistribution and toxicity is critical
for urologic health.

METHODS: Wild-type mice were exposed daily to fluorescently-labeled polystyrene MP via hydrogel cups
for 45 days. MP biodistribution was assessed in blood, urine, kidney, and bladder tissues. Renal function
was evaluated via albumin/creatinine ratio (ACR), histology, and immunofluorescence. Bladder tissue was
analyzed for MP presence and structural changes (Scheme 1).

RESULTS: MP were detected in blood and urine within 2–4 weeks of exposure, confirming systemic
absorption (Fig.1). Histological analysis revealed MP accumulation in glomerular and tubular
compartments (Fig.2). ACR showed a trend toward increased proteinuria in exposed mice, suggesting
early renal dysfunction (Fig. 3). Notably, MP were also identified in bladder tissue, indicating lower urinary
tract involvement. No overt histological damage was observed in the bladder, but MP localization suggests
potential for long-term impact.

title: Verification of renal tissue regeneration using human perinephric fat-derived collagen sheet in a partially nephrectomized animal model
text:
Abstract 20: Verification of renal tissue regeneration
                                                       using human perinephric fat-derived collagen sheet in
                                                       a partially nephrectomized animal model
                                                       Jae Sung Lim, Eun Hye Lee, Bo Hyun Yoon, Minji Jeon, Sang Hee Lee, Jun-Koo Kang, Jae-Wook Chung, Yun-Sok
                                                       Ha, Seock Hwan Choi, Bum Soo Kim, Hyun Tae Kim, Tae-Hwan Kim, Eun Sang Yoo, Tae Gyun Kwon



INTRODUCTION                                        RESULTS
• Limited treatment options for chronic kidney
  disease(CKD),      such      as    dialysis  or
  transplantation, have significant drawbacks.
• This study aims to investigate the potential of
  a collagen sheet derived from human perirenal
  adipose tissue for kidney regeneration.


METHODS
• Collagen sheets were derived from discarded
  perirenal adipose tissues and implanted into
  partially nephrectomized mice.
• A collagen sheet was implanted in the mid-
  pole of the left kidney following partial
  resection of renal parenchyme.
• Renal function, inflammation,      and   tissue
  regeneration were evaluated.

title: Ureteral Wall thickness in Predicting need for Surgical Intervention in Ureteric Calculi =7 mm: Single Centre Retrospective Analysis
text:
Abstract #: 26-9172
                                                                    Ureteral Wall thickness in Predicting need for Surgical Intervention in
                                                                    Ureteric Calculi ≤7 mm: Single Centre Retrospective Analysis

                                                                    Authors : Siddhant Kumar, Surag KR, Anupam Choudhary, Sunil Pillai Bhaskara, Padmaraj Hegde, Arun Chawla
INTRODUCTION
● Ureteric calculi ≤7 mm represent a common therapeutic dilemma -
  generally amenable to medical expulsive therapy (MET), a clinically
  relevant proportion ultimately require surgical intervention.
                                                                             RESULTS
● Accurately identifying patients who will fail MET at initial
  presentation remains a significant challenge - stone size alone
  provides insufficient discriminatory power.
● Ureteral wall thickness (UWT), measurable on NCCT KUB, reflects
  localised oedema and the inflammatory response to stone
  impaction.
● Study Aim: To evaluate UWT as an independent predictor of
  surgical intervention in ureteric calculi ≤7 mm and identify an
  optimal threshold to guide management decisions.


    METHODS




                                                                                                     DISCUSSION
                                                                                                     ● Current EAU/AUA guidelines recommend MET for ureteric stones ≤10 mm, with spontaneous passage
                                                                                                       rates of 68% (<5 mm) and 47% (5–10 mm) [1]
                                                                                                     ● Alpha-blockers improve expulsion rates for larger distal stones, but the SUSPEND trial (Lancet, 2015)
                                                                                                       found no benefit over placebo in a 1,167-patient RCT [2,3]
                                                                                                     ● Stone size and location alone cannot reliably predict MET failure.
                                                                                                     ● UWT reflects mucosal oedema and impaction severity - providing a pathophysiological basis
                                                                                                       for predicting failure independent of stone dimensions
                                                                                                     ● A cutoff of 2.6 mm achieves 80% sensitivity and 76% specificity, derived from the same NCCT KUB
                                                                                                       performed at baseline.

                                                                                                     CONCLUSIONS
                                                                                                     ● UWT is an independent predictor of surgical intervention beyond stone size alone
                                                                                                     ● A threshold of 2.6 mm can guide early triage at first presentation
                                                                                                     ● Routine UWT measurement adds no cost to standard stone assessment
                                                                                                     ● UWT should be incorporated into future ureteric stone management guidelines

                                                                                                     LIMITATIONS
                                                                                                     ● Single-centre retrospective design — prospective multicentre validation warranted
                                                                                                                                                                             ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS
                                                                                                                                                                             Dr Surag KR for his valuable insight

title: Modeling the Impact of Operator Duty Cycle and Irrigation Flow Rate on Thermal Safety During High-Power Laser Lithotripsy
text:
26-8924: Modeling the Impact of Operator Duty Cycle and Irrigation
                                                            Flow Rate on Thermal Safety During High-Power Laser Lithotripsy
                                                           Annika Singh1, Arpit Mishra2, Ph.D., Robert A. Medairos 3, M.D., Michael E. Lipkin 3, M.D., Pei Zhong 2, Ph.D., Charles D. Scales 3, M.D.
                                                           1College of Sciences, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, Georgia

               IP: 26-8924                                 2Thomas Lord Department of Mechanical Engineering and Materials Science, Duke University, Durham, North Carolina
                                                           3Department of Urology, Duke University Medical Center, Durham, North Carolina



                           INTRODUCTION                                                                                                                                    RESULTS
❑ High-power laser lithotripsy improves stone fragmentation
  efficiency
❑ However, intrarenal temperatures >43 °C may cause urothelial
  injury
❑ Temperature rise depends on laser power, irrigation flow rate (IFR),
  and operator duty cycle (ODC).
❑ Knowledge gap: The combined influence of ODC and IFR on
  intrarenal temperature and thermal dose remains poorly
  understood.
❑ Objective: Evaluate how ODC modulation and irrigation flow rate
  influence temperature rise and thermal dose during laser
  lithotripsy.

                          METHODOLOGY
❑ Developed first-order convective heat transfer model
   (adapted from Williams et al., 2021)
❑ Simulated renal collecting system volume: 5.9 mL
❑ Parameters studied
✓ Laser power: 5- 40 W                                                                          ❑ Effect of Duty Cycle on Thermal Dose (CEM43): Duty-cycle modulation reduced thermal dose (CEM43) compared to
✓ Irrigation flow rate (IFR): 0 - 39 mL/min                                                       continuous lasing, despite equal total energy (2400 J). (See Fig. B and E)
✓ Duty cycle modes                                                                              ❑ Effect of Irrigation Flow:
    ❖ 5/5, 10/10, 20/20, 30/30 (on/off seconds)                                                  ✓ Increasing irrigation flow rate (IFR) reduced ΔTmax by 4–100%.
    ❖ Continuous lasing                                                                          ✓ At IFR ≥ 14.5 mL/min, ΔTmax decreased from 12.7 °C (continuous) to 4.4 °C (ODC 5/5), almost ~65% reduction.
❑ Total delivered energy: 2400 J for all conditions                                             ❑ Combined Effects
❑ Outcome metrics                                                                               ✓ Higher laser power increased ΔTmax and CEM43 (Fig. F), while increasing IFR reduced both.
✓ Maximum Absolute temperature (Tmax)                                                           ✓ ODC modulation reduced ΔTmax by 19–91%, depending on laser power and irrigation flow.
✓ Maximum temperature rise (ΔTmax)                                                              ✓ Increasing power approximately doubled ΔTmax, but this increase was mitigated by higher IFR and ODC modulation.
✓ Thermal dose (CEM43)
✓ Model validation using in-vitro temperature measurements.
                                                                                                                                                                   CONCLUSIONS
                                   RESULTS                                                      ✓ Duty-cycle modulation significantly reduces thermal exposure during high-power laser lithotripsy
❑ Model Validation: Model predictions matched experimental                                      ✓ Increasing irrigation flow further limits temperature rise
  temperature profiles (at 40 W with continuous lasing), confirming                             ✓ Combined ODC + adequate irrigation maintains fragmentation energy while improving thermal safety
  accuracy. (See Fig. A and D)                                                                  ❖ Clinical Implication: Real-time duty-cycle control in laser systems may reduce risk of urothelial injury during lithotripsy.
ACKNOWLEDGEMENT: This work was supported in part by the Paired Undergraduate Mentoring Program (PUMP) in Uro-Nephrology. The project builds upon work conducted by Annika Singh during the Summer 2024 PUMP program, under the supervision of Dr. Charles D. Scales.

                                                                                                                        Department of Urology, Loma Linda University Health

                                                        Introduction

•       The global incidence of urolithiasis continues to rise, driven by lifestyle and
        environmental factors. This growing disease burden has led to a corresponding increase
        in endoscopic laser lithotripsy volumes, highlighting the ongoing need for advances in
        procedural safety and technique.
•       During these procedures, air bubbles are frequently introduced into the operative field
        through endoscopic instrument insertion and irrigation delivery.
•       Even a brief laser activation within these air bubbles can cause significant increases in
        temperature, with the potential for protein denaturation (≥60°C) and thermal injury to
        the urinary tract.
•       Air bubble accumulation further impairs endoscopic visualization, requiring continuous
        irrigation flow and drainage through ureteral access sheath to limit build-up.
•       This study evaluates the efficacy of various air elimination systems (AES) in reducing
        endoscopic air bubble burden in a benchtop model. title: Cost-benefit of a urethral catheterisation device (UCD®) for difficult catheter insertion in the Emergency Department
text:
Urethral catheterisation device (UCD®) for difficult catheter insertion in the
Emergency Department
Chong Li Si Alyssa, Zoe Williams1,2, Song Kang1, Alexander Combes1,2, George McClintock2, Jeremy Saad1,2, Ramesh Shanmugasundaram1,2, Varun Bhoopathy1, Brayden March1, Femi E. Ayeni2,3, Isaac Thangasamy1,2,4,
Nicola Jeffery1,2
1 Department of Urology, Nepean Hospital, Sydney, Australia. 2 Nepean Urology Research Group, Sydney, Australia. 3 Nepean Institute of Academic Surgery, Nepean Clinical School, The University of Sydney, Sydney,

Australia. 4 School of Medicine, The University of Sydney, Sydney, Australia.



 Introduction
 Urethral catheterization is a common medical procedure performed in up to
 25% of hospitalized patients. Catheter-associated urethral injury (CAUI)
 occurs in 0.3-1.3% of catheterised males. A urethral catheterisation device
 with an integrated guidewire (Urethrotech UCD®) can facilitate safe and
 successful urethral catheterisation by non-urologists when first-line
 techniques are unsuccessful. This study assesses the implementation of a
 protocol for difficult male urethral catheterisation (DUC) incorporating the
 UCD® in an Australian metropolitan hospital Emergency Department (ED)
 and evaluates the cost-effectiveness of this approach.
                                                                                                                   Urethral catheterisation device (UCD®) - endorsed by the National Institute for Health and Clinical
                                                                                                                                                           Excellence (NICE)




                                                                                Methods
                                                                                A prospective trial was conducted over 18 months in an Australian tertiary hospital Emergency Department. For
                                                                                six months, referrals to urology from the ED for assistance with male DUC or management of CAUI were
                                                                                prospectively audited.

                                                                                A protocol for male DUC was then implemented in the Emergency Department. The protocol mandated use of the
                                                                                UCD® after one failed attempt at male urethral catheterisation. The prospective audit continued for a further eight
                                                                                months after the male DUC protocol was implemented.

                                                                                The success rate of the UCD®, frequency of urology referrals, frequency of CAUI, and the cost of urology
                                                                                involvement was calculated. Care costs were obtained from the hospital finance department.

                                                                                Results
                                                                                In the 6-months without the DUC protocol, there were 10 referrals to urology from ED for assistance with male DUC.
                                                                                CAUIs were sustained in seven out of 10 patients (70%) with DUC. CAUIs included urosepsis (n=3), false passages
                                                                                (n=4), and other urethral trauma (n=2). Management of these complications involved urology admission (n=7),
                                                                                antibiotics (n=8), or a period of urethral catheterisation and outpatient trial of void (n=10).

                                                                                After introduction of the DUC protocol, the UCD® was successful in facilitating DUC in 13 out of 15 patients (87%).
                                                                                CAUI occurred in three out of 15 (20%) patients with DUC (P=0.051). All CAUIs during this period were false passages
                                                                                (n=3). There were three referrals to urology for assistance in performing urethral catheterisation (n=2) or to facilitate
                                                                                outpatient management plans (n=1) (P<0.001).

                                                                                The mean cost of DUC-related care for patients when the UCD® was implemented (successfully or unsuccessfully)
                                                                                was $832 per patient (SD $1286), compared with a mean cost of $2288 (SD $1828) for DUC-related care prior to UCD
                                                                                implementation (P=0.002).




Conclusion
Implementation of the Urethrotech UCD as part of a
                                          ®

DUC protocol in a metropolitan ED reduces patient
morbidity, referrals to urology, and healthcare
expenditure.
                                                                                            Urethrotech UCD® facilitated successful urethral catheterisation without urology assistance
                                                                                                                                            in 10/12 patients (83%).


Disclosures: NIL

(1. Department of Urology, Beijing Friendship hospital, Capital Medical University；2. Institute of Urology, Beijing Municipal Health
Commission.)

 Introduction: Kidney stone recurrence remains a pervasive clinical challenge,
 yet prognostic tools leveraging integrated multi-omics approaches are still
 lacking. This study aimed to develop and validate an integrated model
 predicting kidney stone recurrence by combining gut multi-omics and clinical
 features.

 Method: We conducted a prospective study including patients undergoing
 surgical treatment for kidney stones at Beijing Friendship Hospital between
 July 2022 and April 2024. A comprehensive analytical approach was employed,
 combining 16S rDNA sequencing and LC-MS) of fecal samples with detailed
 clinical profiling. Variable selection was performed using univariate and
 multivariate logistic regression, followed by development of a clinically
 applicable nomogram. Model performance was rigorously assessed through
 ROC analysis and calibration curves, with all statistical analyses executed in R
 software version 4.2.2 (release date: 31 October 2022).

 Result: Among 77 enrolled patients, 38 (49.35%) experienced stone recurrence
 during follow-up. Gut microbiome analysis revealed significantly reduced
 alpha diversity in recurrent cases (K-W test, p < 0.05). LEfSe analysis
 identified distinct microbial signatures characterized by enriched Proteobacteria
 and depleted Firmicutes (LDA > 2.0, p < 0.05). Multivariate analysis
 established Proteobacteria (OR = 0.003, p = 0.030) and Firmicutes (OR =
 36.003, p = 0.025) as independent predictors of recurrence. The resulting
 nomogram demonstrated strong predictive performance(AUC=0.883 training,
 AUC=0.817 validation). Calibration curves showed excellent agreement
 between predicted and observed outcomes (H-L test: p = 0.968 training, p =

title: Androgen-Deprivation Therapy and Nephrolithiasis: Divergent Stone Risk by Prior Stone History in Prostate Cancer
text:
IP12-29: Androgen-Deprivation Therapy and Nephrolithiasis:
                                                   Divergent Stone Risk by Prior Stone History in Prostate Cancer
                                                                                                                                Friday, May 15, 2026

                                                                                                                                Room: 147B
                                                   Far Eastern Memorial Hospital, Taiwan, R.O.C.                                Stone Disease: Epidemiology & Evaluation I




INTRODUCTION
Androgen-deprivation therapy (ADT) is standard for
prostate cancer, but its impact on kidney-stone risk is
uncertain and may differ by prior nephrolithiasis. We
assessed associations between ADT duration and
nephrolithiasis, and secondarily osteoporosis, stratified
by stone history.


METHODS
We conducted a retrospective cohort study in the multi-
institution TriNetX network including 512,489 men with
prostate cancer (ICD-10 C61). To reduce immortal-time
bias, follow-up began 6 months after diagnosis. ADT
within 6 months was classified as long (continuing ≥12
months), short (no records after month 6), or ADT-naïve
(no ADT); patients first exposed after month 6 were
excluded. The primary outcome was first post–time-zero
nephrolithiasis (N20–N23); the secondary outcome was
incident osteoporosis (M80–M81). Within strata defined
by prior nephrolithiasis, we performed 1:1 propensity-
score–matched comparisons between exposure groups
and estimated risks at 12, 24, and 36 months.


RESULTS
In men without prior nephrolithiasis, long ADT was
associated with the lowest cumulative stone risk, short
ADT intermediate, and ADT-naïve the highest. In men
                                                            CONCLUSIONS
with a stone history, long ADT showed the highest           In this large cohort, ADT was linked to heterogeneous kidney-stone risk—lower incident stones in men
recurrence risk, with short ADT generally between long      without prior nephrolithiasis but higher recurrence among stone-formers—while consistently
and naïve. Across strata, osteoporosis risk rose in a       increasing osteoporosis with longer exposure. These findings support proactive bone-health care for
duration-related pattern (long > short > naïve).            all patients on ADT and intensified stone-prevention strategies in those with a stone history.

• This study assessed recurrence, metastasis and cancer-           weighting and imputation. Advanced T stage (HR 2.35; p=0.003),

METHODS                                                            p=0.64), confirming oncologic equivalence under negative
Retrospective single-center analysis (2013–2025) of                margins and proper nodal control. Competing-risks modeling
histologically confirmed SCC. Variables included: pathologic       reaffirmed recurrence as the main driver of CSM (sub-HR 5.22;
(pT/pN), lymphovascular/perineural invasion (LVI/PNI),             95% CI 2.71–10.06; p< 0.001), with strong discrimination
margins, histology, surgery type, ILND, adjuvant therapy,          (Harrell’s C=0.83) and calibration.
recurrence, metastasis and vital status.

DFS and OS were analyzed by Kaplan–Meier and log-rank              CONCLUSIONS
tests, predictors by multivariable Cox regression modeling         Relapse is the key determinant of prognosis in
recurrence as a time-dependent covariate. Fine–Gray                penile SCC and appears to outweigh both the
analysis addressed competing CSM events, and inverse-              extent of surgery and baseline pathological
probability weighting corrected selection bias.                    features. When negative margins and adequate

                                                                   remains an oncologically sound approach. The

                                                                                                                                                     Discussion

• SSI incidence was low (1.2%), consistent with previous reports. Most SSIs were superficial, and deep/organ-space SSIs were rare but clinically significant.
• Bowel injury was the strongest risk factor for SSI, particularly for deep and organ/space infections. Enterobacterales were frequently identified, suggesting a close association with bowel injury.
• Prolonged catheterization (≥8 days) was a key risk factor for UTI and RI, highlighting the importance of early catheter removal.
• RI appeared to be influenced more by patient factors and perioperative management than by antibiotic selection.
• Prophylactic antibiotics within 24 h (1st/2nd generation cephalosporins) were adequate for preventing SSI and UTI. Extended antibiotic use did not provide additional benefit.
• In cases with bowel injury, broad-spectrum antibiotics may be considered, although further evidence is needed.

 This study demonstrates that the urinary peptidome differs between individuals with overactive bladder and healthy controls, revealing biologically plausible peptide
 signatures that may reflect underlying pathophysiology. Enrichment of peptides related to calcium and FAD binding in the OAB cohort suggests altered cellular signaling
 and oxidative pathways. The identification of mitochondrial ribosome- and extracellular superoxide dismutase-derived peptides as discriminators highlights potential
 mechanistic links between oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and bladder overactivity. The findings establish urinary peptidomics as a promising noninvasive
 approach to uncover molecular correlates and candidate biomarkers of overactive bladder.

METHODS                                                                                                                                                                    William C. Nahas, MD, PhD
This prospective, non-randomized study included 49 men with
high-risk prostate cancer undergoing robotic prostatectomy.
                                                                                      PET-PSMA
ICG was injected into the mpMRI-defined index lesion using fusion
guidance, and fluorescence was visualized intraoperatively with the
Firefly® system.

Kidney Stones During Potassium Citrate Therapy                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Endourology, Department of Urology




                                                                                                                                                                                         Uric Acid Kidney Stone Burden During K-Citrate Therapy
INTRODUCTION

Uric acid kidney stones — comprised of uric acid crystals and
precipitated by acidic urine — account for 10-15 % of all cases of
nephrolithiasis1. Multiple factors contribute to the development of uric
acid kidney stones, including hypovolemia, persistently low urine pH, and
hyperuricosuria, as well as comorbidities such as obesity, metabolic




                                                                                                                                                           Stone Volume (mm3)
syndromes, gout, etc. Potassium citrate (K-Citrate) is a first-line therapy
for the prevention and dissolution of uric acid kidney stones 1. K-Citrate
serves to alkalinize urine (aiming for a urinary pH < 6) , with current
guidelines recommending 15 to 30 mEq, 2 or 3 times per day1,2. A
computed tomography (CT) scan is the standard modality for diagnosing
nephrolithiasis, with pure uric acid stones typically measuring ~500
Hounsfield units (HU) 1.


PURPOSE

exists on the impact of stone characteristics and dose variances on
dissolution rates. This study analyzes the influence of K-Citrate dosage,

title: Effect of Preoperative Silodosin on Outcomes of Ureteroscopy for Ureterolithiasis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
text:
IP18-21: Effect of Preoperative Silodosin on Outcomes
                                                               of Ureteroscopy for Ureterolithiasis: A Systematic
                                                               Review and Meta-Analysis
                                                               Godinho N.J.S; Colhado C.H., de Amorim L.G.C.R., Andrade M.A., Vilela M.A.D., Menezes, T.H.F., da Costa S.E.M., Lipkin M.,
                                                               Mazzuchi E.M.



                                      PURPOSE
To perform a systematic review and meta-analysis evaluating the efficacy and safety of
preoperative silodosin in improving ureteroscopy (URS) outcomes for ureterolithiasis.


                                      METHODS
PubMed, EMBASE and Cochrane Central were systematically searched for studies
comparing preoperative silodosin with placebo or ‘no preoperative silodosin’ in patients
undergoing URS for ureteral stones. Primary outcomes included ureteral wall injury,
analgesia use, fever, hematuria, stone-free rate (SFR), operative time, and complications.
Statistical analysis was performed using Review Manager 5.1.7. Study quality and risk of
bias         were           assessed            per          Cochrane              guidelines.
                                                                                                    Figure 1 - PRISMA flow diagram of study screening and selection.
                                       RESULTS
Nine studies, including eight randomized clinical trials, including 960 patients were
analyzed; 450 (46.8%) received silodosin. Compared to controls, silodosin significantly
reduced ureteral injuries (RR 0.30; 95% CI: 0.18–0.49; p < 0.00001) and operative time
(MD -17.72 minutes; 95% CI: -24.72 to -10.72; p < 0.00001). It also lowered analgesia
needs (RR 0.35; 95% CI: 0.16–0.75; p = 0.007), with trends toward reduced fever (RR
0.67; 95% CI: 0.36–1.22; p = 0.19) and hematuria (RR 0.57; 95% CI: 0.32–1.02; p =
0.06). In studies with ≥10 days of preoperative use, silodosin significantly improved SFR
(RR 1.17; 95% CI: 1.10–1.26; p < 0.00001).

                                   CONCLUSION
Preoperative silodosin reduces ureteral injuries, operative time, and complications,
supporting its use to improve safety and efficiency of URS for ureterolithiasis.

title: Predicting Success of Non-Operative Management in Renal Trauma: Accuracy of CT-Based Grading Systems
text:
IP19-23: Predicting Success of Non-Operative Management in Renal
                                                     Trauma: Accuracy of CT-Based Grading Systems
                                                     Authors: Silva P., Severo L., Cunha J., Caceiro R., Lança M., Almeida R., Gouveia S., Campos
                                                     Pinheiro L.
                                                     ULS S José; Nova Medical School                                              Lisbon, Portugal



INTRODUCTION                                                                         RESULTS
Non-operative management (NOM) has become the preferred strategy for                 Study characteristics:
hemodynamically stable renal trauma, but outcome prediction remains uncertain,       • 11 studies (5 high-grade only; 3 all grades; 3 unspecified), total ≈ 3 500 patients.
especially in high-grade injuries. This systematic review evaluated the predictive   • 8 retrospective, 2 prospective, 1 multi-institutional.
accuracy of CT-based grading systems and radiologic parameters for determining       Non-operative success:
NOM success across renal trauma severities.                                          • High-grade injuries (III–V): 52–92 % success.
                                                                                     • All-grade cohorts: 80–92 % success.
                                                                                     • AAST/CT grade predictive in 4 of 6 studies (OR up to 7.36).
METHODS                                                                              Quantitative accuracy:
A semantic systematic search using Pubmed, Embase and Scopus. Eleven met             • AUC = 0.83–0.88; sensitivity 90.5 %, specificity 78 %.
inclusion criteria: human studies using CT-based grading (AAST or equivalent),       • Active bleeding or contrast extravasation consistently predicted NOM failure.
reporting NOM outcomes and predictive accuracy. Extracted variables included         • Hematoma diameter > 3 cm and parenchymal devascularization > 25 % strongly associated
injury grade, CT features, NOM success rate, and diagnostic metrics (AUC,              with adverse outcomes.
sensitivity, specificity, OR/RR).
                                                                                     Combined predictive models:
                                                                                     • Variables most frequently included: injury grade, hemodynamic stability, hematoma size, and
                                                                                       extravasation.
                                                                                     • Best model (Kim et al., 2021): AUC 0.88; intrarenal contrast extravasation OR 7.41.
                                                                                     Functional outcomes:
                                                                                     • Two studies linked > 25 % parenchymal devascularization to long-term renal function loss.
                                                                                     • Successful NOM preserved renal units in > 75 % of cases (van der Wilden et al., 2013).



                                                                                     CONCLUSIONS
                                                                                     CT-based grading provides moderately accurate prediction of NOM success (AUC ≈ 0.85), but
                                                                                     precision increases when specific CT parameters—such as hematoma size, active bleeding, and
                                                                                     devascularization—are integrated. AAST grade alone underestimates risk in complex injuries.
                                                                                     Standardization of CT reporting and inclusion of quantitative markers could enhance decision-
                                                                                     making and reduce unnecessary nephrectomies. Prospective validation of AI-assisted CT
                                                                                     nomograms should be prioritized to optimize trauma triage and renal preservation

                                                 Mark Farha1,2, Jacob Lang1,2, Gal Wald1,2, Ali Ghasemzadeh1, Vincent D’Andrea1, Noah Frydenlund1, Eugene Pietzak1

                            Introduction                                                                                                                        Results
 • “BCG-Exposed” Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer (NMIBC):                                                                                                         a.
   High-Grade (HG) recurrence within 24 mos of prior BCG
   exposure and not meeting strict “BCG-Unresponsive” Criteria
