title: Global Practices and Perceptions in Stone Burden Assessment: Results from the International Survey on Stone Volume Measurement
text:
IP63-24: Global Practices and Perceptions in Stone Burden Assessment: Results
                                          from the International Survey on Stone Volume Measurement

                                                                     Akinbo F1, Pauchard F 1, Larrañaga M2, Salvadó JA1,2
                                1University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center, Case Western Reserve University, School of Medicine
                                                             2Universidad Finis Terrae, Facultad de Medicina, Santiago de Chile




                         INTRODUCTION                                                                                                                     RESULTS

• Preoperative stone burden measurement drives procedure choice,
  access planning, operative time estimates, and outcome reporting.              • 252 urologists from six continents; 91.7% were attending urologists.
• Despite stones being 3D, routine practice and guidelines still rely mainly     • 83% routinely use maximum diameter; only 27% use any volumetric
  on maximum linear diameter.                                                      metric.
• Linear sizing shows meaningful variability and becomes less reliable as        • Among volumetry users, geometric formulas (sphere/ellipsoid) were
  stones get larger or more irregular.                                             most common (62%); 3D segmentation/PACS tools were rare (<10%).
• Geometric volume estimates (sphere/ellipsoid) help but remain                  • Most reported <5 minutes per case for volume; 82% agreed volume
  imprecise compared with CT-based segmentation.                                   better represents stone burden than diameter.
• Semi-automated and AI tools can generate fast, accurate volumes, but           • Volumetry use was higher in <10 years practice (p=0.04) and academic
  real-world adoption and PACS/EHR integration remain limited and                  settings (p<0.05); 87% would adopt if automated tools were available
  poorly quantified.


                             OBJECTIVE
This study aimed to characterize current global practices,
preferences, and perceived barriers related to stone volume
assessment among urologists.

                             METHODS
We conducted an anonymous, web-based cross-sectional survey of
urologists and trainees involved in stone care (September to
November 2025), distributed via the EAU Urolithiasis Section,
Endourological Society, and other professional networks. The
SurveyMonkey questionnaire assessed demographics, primary
preoperative sizing metric (diameter, volume, or both), volumetric
methods used, CT protocol factors, time required per case,
perceived feasibility, attitudes, laser performance metrics, and
open-text barriers, with branching to show CT- and volume-specific                                                                                  CONCLUSIONS
items only when relevant.
The primary outcome was the preferred preoperative stone burden
metric; secondary outcomes included tool use, workflow time,                      • Global survey shows a clear implementation gap between evidence-supported perceptions and routine stone burden measurement
feasibility, and barriers. Responses were summarized as frequencies                practices
and percentages with varying denominators, and compared by
experience (<10 vs ≥10 years), fellowship status, and practice setting            • Although most urologists view volumetric metrics as superior, adoption remains limited by workflow friction and tool accessibility.
using chi-square or Fisher’s exact tests (two-sided p<0.05); analyses             • Standardized, automated, rapid volumetric solutions are needed to enable consistent measurement and reporting across institutions.
were performed in R. The study was exempt human subjects
research.

                              Elizabeth Gurt Lynch MD¹, Pablo Suarez BS¹, James F. Smith MD MS¹,², Yi Li MD¹
                              ¹UCSF Department of Urology, San Francisco, CA | ²Fellow Health, San Leandro, CA


INTRODUCTION
Adolescent and young adult (AYA) cancer patients face critical
fertility preservation decisions during a vulnerable time.
Treatment urgency, emotional distress, and financial barriers
create challenges to informed decision-making. Despite ASRM
recommendations for comprehensive fertility preservation
counseling, patients receive inconsistent guidance due to absent
standardized protocols and specialty variability. This study
compares sperm cryopreservation counseling by Reproductive
Endocrinology and Infertility (REI) specialists and urologists for
AYA cancer patients.


METHODS




                                                                                                 CONCLUSIONS
                                                                                                 Urologists were more responsive to social and financial
                                                                                                 factors—partnership status, mortality risk, insurance
                                                                                                 coverage, and orchiectomy—while REI specialists
                                                                                                 maintained more standardized approaches. Patients may
                                                                                                 receive substantially different fertility preservation guidance
                                                                                                 depending on the specialist consulted, highlighting the need
                                                                                                 for evidence-based, standardized counseling protocols for
                                                                                                 AYA cancer patients.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       disease complexity
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     • Long-term retreatment prediction showed weaker external performance.
                   Fig 1. Overview of Study Design                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   • Retreatment is a pragmatic endpoint influenced by recurrence biology, symptoms,
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       surveillance, follow-up duration, and institutional thresholds for intervention

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     Limitations
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     • External performance may reflect differences in case mix, surgical practice, follow-up
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       patterns, and outcome definitions
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     • Retreatment may underestimate true recurrence and vary across practice settings
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     • Baseline predictors do not capture postoperative symptoms, uroflow/PVR,
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       cystoscopy findings, or patient preference

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     Future directions
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     • Build prospective, multi-institutional aUSD databases with standardized data
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       collection and long-term follow-up
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     • Harmonize definitions of recurrence, retreatment, and functional success across
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       centers
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     • Standardize collection of clinically meaningful postoperative data, including
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       cystoscopy, uroflow/PVR, symptoms, and PROMs
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     • Use higher-quality longitudinal data to develop dynamic prediction models and
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       patient-facing risk calculators

title: Urinary adverse events after robot-assisted versus non-robotic radical prostatectomy in Medicare beneficiaries
text:
IP68-01:  Urinary   Adverse  Events   Following   Robotic   versus
   Evolving Risk of Urinary Adverse Events Across Localized Prostate Cancer Treatments:
Non-Robotic    Radical Prostatectomy
   A Propensity-Weighted                   in Medicare Beneficiaries
                          SEER-Medicare Analysis
MarvinKevin D. Li, Marvin
       N. Carlisle,       N. Li,
                    Kevin D. Carlisle,
                                 BehzadStephanie Jarosek,
                                         Abbasi, Phillip W. Hiren V. Patel,Frankiewicz,
                                                            Chu, Mikolaj    Anna Faris, Stephanie
                                                                                        Sean P. Elliot, MatthewLynn
                                                                                                  L. Jarosek,   R. Cooperberg, Peter
                                                                                                                    Leng, Anna R.    R. Carroll,
                                                                                                                                  Faris, BenjaminBenjamin N. Breyer
                                                                                                                                                   N. Breyer



                           Introduction & Objective                                                                      Figure 1: Cumulative Incidence of Any UAE
 • Urinary adverse events (UAEs) after radical prostatectomy (RP) drive
   significant morbidity and reinterventions.
 • Comparative data for robot-assisted (RARP) vs. non-robotic (non-RARP) in
   older men, particularly in the mature robotic era, remain limited.
 • Widespread RARP adoption necessitates clearer understanding of long-term
   functional outcome profiles compared to non-RARP approaches.
 • Objective: compare RARP vs. non-RARP postoperative cumulative incidence
   and adjusted hazards of UAEs and related procedures.



                                           Methods
 • Design: Retrospective SEER-Medicare (2010-2018) cohort study.
 • Population: 17,441 Medicare beneficiaries (≥66 yrs) with localized prostate
   cancer treated with RP.
 • Groups:
   • RARP:    14,769 (84.7%)
   • Non-RARP: 2,672 (15.3%)
 • Outcome: Any postoperative UAE (defined by prespecified codes), UAE
                                                                                                                  Figure 2: Adjusted Hazard Ratios for Specific UAEs
   subtypes, and subsequent urethral/bladder procedures.
 • Analysis: Cumulative incidence (Kaplan-Meier) and multivariable Cox
   proportional hazards models, adjusting for age, race, income, year, tumor
   stage/grade, baseline UAE, and Charlson comorbidity.



                                             Results
 • Primary Outcome: RARP was associated with a 50% reduction in the
   hazard of any postoperative UAE.
    • Overall Rate: 7.7% (RARP) vs. 15.3% (Non-RARP)
    • aHR: 0.50 (95% CI 0.45-0.57), p<0.001
 • Driving Factor: This RARP benefit was driven by a ~70-80% reduction in
   Bladder Outlet Obstruction (BOO) and related procedures.
    • BOO diagnosis: aHR 0.27
    • Bladder Neck Incision: aHR 0.20
 • Non-Factor: No differences in incontinence rates or subsequent procedures.
    • Incontinence Diagnosis: aHR 0.97 (95% CI 0.75-1.26)




                                        Conclusions
 • In this large, contemporary Medicare beneficiary cohort, RARP displayed half
   the hazard of experiencing any UAE compared to non-RARP approaches.
 • This benefit is driven by a dramatic reduction in BOO and related                                                                                    Key Takeaway
   interventions, not by different incontinence incidence.                                                     • RARP is associated with half the risk of any UAE (aHR 0.50).
 • These population-level data inform patient counseling and quality                                           • Large reductions in Bladder Outlet Obstruction (aHR 0.27) drive this benefit.
   benchmarking in older men, highlighting a key advantage of robotic
   approaches in the mature surgical era.                                                                      • No difference was found in incontinence rates (aHR 0.97).

INTRODUCTION                                                                            RESULTS
Accurate characterization of adrenal tumors is critical for treatment planning in       Study characteristics:
urology and endocrinology. Conventional imaging modalities have limited
                                                                                        8 retrospective studies (4 multicentre, 3 single-centre; n = 90–1,146 patients).
specificity for differentiating benign from malignant lesions. Radiomics and
                                                                                        • All used radiomics-based AI models, including LASSO regression, Extra Trees, SVM, logistic
artificial intelligence (AI) have emerged as promising non-invasive tools for
                                                                                           regression, and deep learning (ResNet-50).
quantitative CT-based tumor characterization. This systematic review evaluates
                                                                                        • External validation was performed in 3 studies; 4 used combined radiomics-clinical models.
the diagnostic performance, generalizability, and clinical applicability of radiomics
                                                                                        • Diagnostic performance:
and AI models for adrenal tumor differentiation.
                                                                                        • AUC range: 0.79–0.98 across tasks.
                                                                                        • F1 score: 0.96 (pheochromocytoma vs adenoma).
                                                                                        • Sensitivity: 0.81–0.999; Specificity: 0.733–1.00.
METHODS                                                                                 • Combined radiomics-clinical models consistently outperformed imaging-only models.
A systematic semantic search using Elicit (Semantic Scholar + OpenAlex)                 • Deep learning and support vector machine approaches achieved AUCs 0.86–0.90 for metastatic
                                                                                           risk prediction.
identified eight eligible studies (2020–2025) assessing radiomics or AI-based CT
models for adrenal tumor characterization. Inclusion criteria:                          Generalizability: Three studies demonstrated strong external validation, maintaining high
• Original human studies with histopathological or long-term clinical confirmation,     diagnostic accuracy across independent datasets. Limitations included small sample size, class
• Diagnostic accuracy metrics (AUC, sensitivity, specificity),                          imbalance, and non-standardized imaging protocols, which may limit reproducibility.
• Differentiation of adrenal tumor subtypes (adenoma, pheochromocytoma,
   adrenocortical carcinoma, metastasis, aldosteroneproducing adenoma).
Data extracted: model type, validation strategy, diagnostic metrics, and                CONCLUSIONS
integration with clinical or pathological features. Bias was assessed using
adapted QUADAS-2 criteria.                                                              Radiomics and AI-based CT models demonstrate high diagnostic accuracy (AUC 0.79–0.98) for
                                                                                        differentiating adrenal tumor subtypes, rivaling or exceeding conventional imaging. Integrating
                                                                                        clinical or pathological data further enhances model performance. Despite encouraging results,
                                                                                        standardization, larger multicenter validation, and integration into clinical decision workflows are
                                                                                        essential before widespread adoption in urological oncology.

INTRODUCTION                                                           RESULTS
Germline genetic testing (GGT) is recommended for patients             A total of 3614 pts with RCC and 6985 cancer-unaffected pts were included.
(pts) with renal cell carcinoma (RCC) and bilateral/multifocal         In the RCC cohort, 50% were female and mean age at testing was 55 years.
disease, specific variant histology, a diagnosis < 46 years old, or    In the cancer-free cohort, 84% were female and the mean age at testing was 66.
a family history of renal neoplastic syndrome. Retrospective           The PGV prevalence was 8.7% in the RCC cohort and 8.9% in the cancer-unaffected
studies of selected cohorts with advanced disease or                   cohort. Multivariable analysis of any PGVs were similar in the RCC vs cancer-
suggestive personal/family histories show a pathogenic/likely          unaffected cohorts (OR 0.93; 95% CI 0.79-1.10). However, PGVs in RCC
pathogenic germline variant (PGV) prevalence of 5-18%.                 predisposition genes were enriched in the RCC cohort vs cancer-unaffected cohort
However, the prevalence of PGVs and clinical utility of GGT in         (OR 2.73; 95% CI 1.91-3.92) and PGVs in DDR genes were reduced in the RCC cohort
unselected cohorts of pts with RCC remains largely unknown.            vs cancer-unaffected cohort (OR 0.68; 95% CI 0.55-0.83).



METHODS
All pts with an ICD-10 diagnosis code of RCC who underwent
hereditary cancer multi-gene panel testing (MGPT) through
Ambry Genetics from 2019-2021 were identified; clinician-
reported clinical history was abstracted for those with PGVs.
A cancer-unaffected cohort of pts who underwent MGPT during
the same timeframe was also identified, excluding those
younger than 60 years old. This analysis focused on PGVs in 67
genes, including 13 RCC predisposition genes, 20 DNA damage
repair (DDR) genes, and 34 other genes.
Multivariable logistic regression was used to assess the
association between PGV status and RCC diagnosis, adjusting
for age at testing, race, and sex at birth.

        CONCLUSIONS
        The overall prevalence of PGVs was approximately 9% in both RCC and cancer-unaffected cohorts. RCC predisposition genes were enriched
        in pts with RCC and DDR genes were enriched in cancer-unaffected pts. These findings support broader implementation of GGT for pts with
        RCC to guide screening for additional malignancies, management in advanced disease, and cascade genetic testing for family members.

title: Mobile-based Assessment of Entrustable Professional Activities in  Urology Training: Implementation and Outcomes
text:
IP72-01: Mobile-based Assessment of Entrustable
                                                                                                                                                         Professional Activities in Urology Training:
                                                                                                                                                         Implementation and Outcomes
                                                                                                                                                         Fabian J. Aschwanden1,2, Luca Afferi1,2, Lukas Kandler3, Adrian P. Marty3, Philipp Baumeister¹, Agostino Mattei1,2,
                                                                                                                                                         Marko Kozomara1,2, Christian D. Fankhauser1,2,3
                                                                                                                                                         1 Faculty of Health Sciences and Medicine, University of Lucerne, Lucerne, Switzerland
                                                                                                                                                         2 Clinic for Urology, University Teaching and Research Hospital of the University of Lucerne, Lucerne, Switzerland
                                                                                                                                                         3 University of Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland




INTRODUCTION                                                                                                                                                 RESULTS & CONCLUSIONS
Competency-based medical education is shifting surgical
training from time- and volume-based progression toward
documented competence in defined clinical activities.
Entrustable professional activities provide a structured
framework for assessing observable units of professional
practice. However, implementation in daily clinical training is
often limited by delayed feedback, inconsistent assessment
criteria, and difficulty tracking residents’ progress over time.
Mobile technology may facilitate real-time workplace-based
assessment by making feedback faster, more frequent, and
easier to document.
Objective: To implement and evaluate a smartphone-based EPA
assessment tool for real-time feedback and competency tracking
in urology residency training.


METHODS
A two-phase implementation project was conducted at a Swiss
urology training institution.
Phase 1:
• A consultant working group defined 46 urology-specific EPAs
   covering general, specialty-specific, preoperative,
   intraoperative, postoperative, emergency, and nonoperative
   technical tasks.
Phase 2:
• The preparedEPA smartphone application was introduced into
   routine clinical training. The app was installed by 13 trainees
   and 10 supervisors.
• After completing an EPA under supervision, the trainee initiated
   an assessment in the app. Both trainee and supervisor
   independently rated task complexity and the required level of
   future supervision using a five-level entrustment-supervision
   scale: observe, direct supervision, indirect supervision, distant
   supervision, and supervise others.
• Assessment characteristics were analyzed descriptively.
   Agreement between trainees and supervisors was evaluated
   using weighted Cohen’s κ and Fleiss’ κ.
DISCLOSURES
This work was supported by a 2023 Gilead SAKK Expanding Horizons in Oncology Award to Christian D. Fankhauser.
Adrian P. Marty and Lukas Kandler serve on the board of directors at PrecisionED Ltd., the company developing the preparedEPA application.
Generative AI was used to support the visual structuring and graphical preparation of this poster; all scientific content was reviewed and verified by
the authors.

title: Protective role of bone-modifying agents against febrile neutropenia in patients with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer receiving upfront docetaxel
text:
Protective role of bone-modifying agents against febrile neutropenia
                         in patients with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer receiving
                         upfront docetaxel
                         S. Tazawa¹, N. Fujita¹, F. Yoneyama¹, T. Ichiyama¹, S. Hosogoe¹, K. Togashi¹, H. Asanuma¹, H. Horiguchi¹, Y. Ishibashi¹, W. Fukuokaya²,
                         T. Yanagisawa², S. Narita³, T. Kimura², T. Habuchi³, S. Hatakeyama¹                                                                        I have no COI to
   IP73-02               1) Hirosaki University Graduate School of Medicine, Urology, Hirosaki, Japan ; 2) The Jikei University, School of Medicine, Urology,           disclose.
                         Tokyo, Japan ; 3) Akita University School of Medicine, Urology, Akita, Japan                                                              Shunsuke Tazawa


  Introduction & Objectives
  The introduction of upfront docetaxel, including triplet therapy, has significantly transformed the systemic treatment landscape for metastatic hormone-sensitive
  prostate cancer (mHSPC). However, it can cause severe hematological toxicities, including febrile neutropenia (FN). Given the close relationship between
  neutropenia and bone marrow function, and the role of bone-modifying agents (BMAs) in modulating the bone marrow microenvironment, we hypothesized that
  patients receiving combined therapy with docetaxel and BMAs may have a lower risk of FN compared to those receiving docetaxel alone.
  Materials & Methods
  This retrospective study included 214 patients with mHSPC who received upfront docetaxel, including darolutamide-based triplet therapy, between December
  2015 and September 2025. FN was defined according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0. BMAs included zoledronic acid and
  denosumab. Multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed to identify risk factors for FN. Additionally, subgroup analyses were conducted to evaluate
  the association between BMA use and FN incidence across clinical subgroups, including age, docetaxel dose, and extent of disease (EOD) score.
  Results
  The median age and docetaxel dose were 71 years and 70 mg/m², respectively. Of the 214 patients, 115 (54%) received BMAs during mHSPC treatment. FN of
  grade 3 or higher occurred in 28 patients (13%). The incidence rate of FN was significantly lower in patients treated with BMAs compared to those who were not
  (Fig. A). In univariable analyses, higher docetaxel dose was significantly associated with increased FN risk, while BMA use was significantly associated with
  reduced risk (Fig. B). In contrast, extent of disease score and primary prophylactic administration of granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) were not
  significantly associated with FN. After adjusting for age, only BMA use remained significantly associated with FN. Subgroup analyses revealed that the protective
  effect of BMAs was not observed in patients receiving lower docetaxel doses or those with lower bone metastasis burden.




Conclusion
FN occurred in 13% of patients with mHSPC receiving upfront docetaxel. BMA use may be associated with a reduced risk of FN,
although its benefit may be limited in patients with lower chemotherapy intensity or disease burden.

title: Cost-saving potential of reduced-dose androgen receptor signaling inhibitors without loss of efficacy in non-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer
text:
IP73-09: Cost-saving potential of reduced-dose androgen
                                                      receptor signaling inhibitors without loss of efficacy in non-
                                                      metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer
               I have no COI with regard              R. Tanaka , N.Fujita , S. Kato , Y. Kawashima , M. Shinohara , R. Tabata , D. Noro , Y. Suzuki , S. Sato , S. Hatakeyama
                                                               1          1         2              2              2           3         1           1         2                1

                   to our presentation.               1Hirosaki University Graduate School of Medicine, Urology, Hirosaki, Japan, 2Ageo Central General Hospital, Urology, Ageo, Japan,

                      Ryuma Tanaka                    3Sano Kosei General Hospital, Urology, Sano, Japan


Introduction & Objectives
The introduction of novel androgen receptor signaling inhibitors (ARSIs) has significantly transformed the systemic treatment landscape for non-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (nmCRPC). However,
ARSI therapy is associated with substantial adverse events (AEs) and increased medical costs. Dose reduction may offer a strategy to mitigate AEs and reduce costs, yet the efficacy, safety, and cost-effectiveness
of reduced-dose ARSIs in nmCRPC remain unclear.
Materials & Methods
This multicenter retrospective study included 251 patients with nmCRPC who received ARSI therapy. Patients were categorized into two groups based on the initial ARSI dose: reduced-dose group (n = 46) and full-
dose group (n = 205). Prostate-specific antigen progression-free survival (PSA-PFS), metastasis-free survival (MFS), and overall survival (OS) were compared between groups. Monthly medical costs for first ARSI
treatment were also evaluated.
Results
The median age at nmCRPC diagnosis was 77 years, with a median follow-up duration of 46 months. Figure A illustrates sequential changes in ARSI dosage, including distribution and transition patterns. The rates
of any PSA response, PSA decline ≥50%, and PSA decline ≥90% were comparable between the full-dose and reduced-dose groups (85% vs. 89%, P = 0.640; 74% vs. 76%, P = 0.785; 46% vs. 35%, P = 0.171,
respectively). No significant differences were observed in PSA-PFS (Fig. B), MFS (Fig. C), or OS (Fig. D) between the two groups. After adjusting for confounding variables, reduced initial ARSI dose was not
significantly associated with shorter MFS (P = 0.984, hazard ratio: 0.992, 95% confidence interval: 0.467–2.107). The incidence rates of any-grade and grade ≥3 AEs did not differ significantly between the groups
(33% vs. 24%, P = 0.171; 3.9% vs. 4.3%, P = 1.000). Median monthly medication costs for first ARSI treatment were significantly lower in the reduced-dose group compared to the full-dose group (Fig. E),
representing an approximate 40% cost reduction.
Conclusions
Reduced-dose ARSI therapy demonstrated comparable efficacy and safety to full-dose treatment in patients with nmCRPC, while significantly lowering medication costs. Dose reduction may be a viable strategy to
enhance cost-effectiveness without compromising clinical outcomes.

title: Trends and risk factor for non-prostate cancer mortality in patients with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer receiving upfront therapy
text:
Trends and risk factor for non-prostate cancer mortality in
                                                                  patients with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer
                                                                  receiving upfront therapy
                                                                  Fumiya Yoneyama 1 , Naoki Fujita 1 , Daisuke Noro 1 , Syunsuke Tazawa 1 , Takaki Ichiyama 1 , Keita Ishimoto 1 , Wataru Fukuokaya 2 ,
                                                                  Takafumi Yanagisawa 2 , Shintaro Narita 3 , Takahiro Kimura 2 , Tomonori Habuchi 3 , Shingo Hatakeyama 1

             IP73-15                                              1. Hirosaki University Graduate School of Medicine, Hirosaki, Japan
                                                                  2. The Jikei University, School of Medicine, Tokyo, Japan
                                                                  3. Akita University School of Medicine, Akita, Japan




 BACKGROUND
 The introduction of upfront therapy, including docetaxel and novel androgen receptor signaling inhibitors (ARSIs), has significantly transformed the systemic treatment landscape for
 metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC) and improved patient prognosis. Consequently, the proportion of deaths from non-prostate cancer (non-PC death) may
 increase. However, the trends and risk factors associated with non-PC death in patients with mHSPC receiving upfront therapy remain poorly understood.



 METHODS
 This multicenter retrospective study included 1,262 patients with mHSPC who received upfront therapy between December 2015 and September 2025. Treatment regimens included
 docetaxel, ARSIs, or a combination of docetaxel and darolutamide. We compared the proportion of non-PC deaths among all-cause deaths between patients diagnosed with mHSPC
 during two time periods: 2015–2019 and 2020–2025. Multivariable analyses were conducted to identify risk factors for non-PC death, adjusting for PC death as a competing risk using
 the Fine-Gray subdistribution hazards model.


RESULTS
The median age and follow-up duration were 73 years and 25 months, respectively. Among the 1,262 patients, 378 (30%) developed metastatic castration-resistant PC (mCRPC), 180
(14%) died from PC, and 79 (6.3%) died from other causes. Among the 884 patients who did not progress to mCRPC, 22 (2.5%) died from PC and 58 (6.6%) died from other causes. In
contrast, among the 378 patients who developed mCRPC, 158 (42%) died from PC and 21 (5.6%) died from other causes (Fig. A). The proportion of non-PC deaths among all-cause
deaths did not differ significantly between patients diagnosed in 2015–2019 and those diagnosed in 2020–2025 (Fig. B). Figure C illustrates the cumulative incidence of PC death and
non-PC death. In multivariable Fine-Gray competing risk regression analysis, older age and lower body mass index (BMI) were significantly associated with an increased risk of non-PC
death. The adjusted subdistribution hazard ratios were 1.047 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.022–1.074, P < 0.001) for age and 0.907 (95% CI 0.838–0.982, P = 0.017) for BMI (Fig. D).

title: Real-world treatment patterns and outcomes of novel androgen receptor signaling inhibitor therapy in non-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer
text:
Real-world treatment patterns and outcomes of novel androgen receptor signaling
 inhibitor therapy in non-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer
N. Fujita , Y. Kawashima , M. Shinohara , R. Tabata , H. Miura , K, Okita ,S. Sato , and S. Hatakeyama
         1,*            2              2           3          1          1        2                    1                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            IP73-17
1Department of Urology, Hirosaki University Graduate School of Medicine, Hirosaki, Japan; 2Department of Urology, Ageo Central General Hospital, Ageo, Japan; 3Sano Kosei General Hospital, Sano, Japan

*Corresponding author’s E-mail address: naonao707012@hirosaki-u.ac.jp
Background
     Although three pivotal phase III trials have demonstrated significant oncological benefits of novel androgen receptor signaling inhibitors (ARSIs) in patients with non-metastatic castration-resistant prostate
     cancer (nmCRPC), their translation into routine clinical practice remains incompletely characterized. In particular, real-world treatment patterns, safety profiles, and long-term outcomes associated with ARSI
     use in diverse patient populations have been sparsely documented.
     Understanding how these agents are adopted and perform outside of controlled trial settings is essential for optimizing nmCRPC management and informing clinical decision-making.
Methods
 This multicenter retrospective study evaluated 318 consecutive patients with nmCRPC treated between 2001 and 2024.
     Trends in the use of novel ARSIs were analyzed.
     Adverse events associated with novel ARSIs were assessed using the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0.
     Multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression analyses were conducted to evaluate the effects of novel ARSIs on metastasis-free survival (MFS) and overall survival (OS).

 INTRODUCTION                                                       RESULTS
 To evaluate the feasibility and safety of the Toumai®
 robotic system in urologic surgery through analysis of
 the first 100 consecutive procedures performed in a
 European referral robotic centre.




 METHODS
 • Prospective cohort (May–October 2025) at a European
 referral robotic centre

 • Consecutive patients undergoing Toumai® robotic
 urologic surgery

 • Procedures: RARP, RAPN, RARN, RARC

 • All surgeries performed by experienced robotic
 surgeons

 • Data collected in a dedicated prospective database:
 - Demographic
 - Perioperative
 - Early postoperative




CONCLUSIONS
Our experience highlights that urologic procedures
performed with the Toumai® robotic system are feasible
and safe, confirming its suitability for routine clinical use in
a high-volume setting.

title: Functional Outcomes of Minimally Invasive Treatments for Benign Prostatic Obstruction: A Systematic Review and Updated Network Meta-analysis
text:
Minimally Invasive Treatments for Benign Prostatic
                                                                   Obstruction: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis
                                                                   of 3-Month Outcomes
                                                                   Godinho N.J.S., Onofre J.C.M., Colhado C.H., Vilela M.A.D., Menezes T.H.F., Andrade Junior M.A., Rodrigues H.G., Donalisio da Silva
                                                                   R.




                                         PURPOSE
The surgical management of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) requires balancing the proven
efficacy of conventional procedures with the improved safety and recovery profiles offered by
novel minimally invasive surgical therapies (MISTs). As the therapeutic landscape continues to
evolve and head-to-head comparative data remain limited, this study systematically evaluates the
efficacy and safety outcomes of both established and emerging MISTs to inform evidence-based
clinical decision-making.

                                         METHODS
PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane were systematically searched (2015–2025) for RCTs comparing
MISTs in BPH patients, following PRISMA guidelines. Outcomes included Qmax, PVR, IPSS,
IPSS-QoL, IIEF, MSHQ-EjD, and safety. A Bayesian random-effects network meta-analysis was
conducted using MetaInsight 2.0, generating 95% credible intervals (CrI) and SUCRA rankings.



                                         RESULTS
This network meta-analysis included 36 RCTs (4,782 patients) evaluating 14 interventions.
Aquablation showed the greatest effect in IPSS (MD −8.82; 95% CrI −14.91 to −2.73) and Qmax
(MD 16.88 ml/s; 95% CrI 9.69 to 23.97) versus sham. iTIND and Optilume did not demonstrate
superiority over sham for IPSS. In the class-level analysis, Ablative therapies were the only class    Figure 1 - PRISMA flow diagram of study screening and selection.
statistically superior to sham (MD −7.20; 95% CrI −10.46 to −3.93) and ranked first overall for
IPSS (SUCRA 98.68%) and IPSS-QoL (SUCRA 84.56%). Enucleation achieved the greatest PVR
reduction (ThuLEP SUCRA 95.08%). Resection was the only class with significant ejaculatory
deterioration (MD −3.16; 95% CrI −6.17 to −0.11), while Stent/Implant/Endoluminal therapies
preserved ejaculatory function (MD −3.20; 95% CrI −5.40 to −0.90).


                                      CONCLUSION
Among MISTs for BPH, Aquablation and Ablative therapies provided the greatest IPSS
improvement, while Enucleation led in PVR reduction. Stent/Implant/Endoluminal techniques
offered the best ejaculatory preservation but showed limited urinary efficacy, with iTIND and
Optilume not differing from sham. These findings highlight the importance of outcome-driven
procedure selection and transparent counseling on functional trade-offs in tailoring BPH surgical      Figure 2 - IPSS network meta-analysis: (A) SUCRA cumulative ranking curves by procedure; (B) forest plot

 INTRODUCTION                                    RESULTS

Alfonso Santangelo¹; Alex Stephens2; Carlo Silvani¹; Jack Considine¹; Nicholas Saaedi¹; Tavan Zadeh¹; Bassel Salka¹, Emanuele Montanari 3; Mario Catanzaro 4,Nicola Nicolai4; Andrea Salonia5; Alberto Briganti5; Francesco

University, Unit of Urology - Division of Oncology -Gianfranco Soldera Prostate Cancer Lab, Milan, Italy




INTRODUCTION                                                                                                                   RESULTS
Although the role of PSA in prostate cancer (PCa) screening remains controversial
guidelines have always clearly established that a patient with an elevated PSA (≥4 ng/ml)
need further diagnostic work-up. However, in clinical practice these patients are not                                                                   Covariate                            HR (95% CI)

always worked-up in a timely manner and the impact of that on their oncological outcomes                                                            centrally reviewed and
is scarcely addressed in literature. We hypothesize that missing or not perform a timely                                                            graded using PI-QUAL
work-up in these individuals leads to worst cancer control outcomes.                                                                                v2 and PI-RADS v2.1

 MATERIALS & METHODS

                                 7,003 pt with PSA > 4 ng/ml tested at one of
                                 Henry Ford Health System facilities (MI, USA)
                                 between 1995 and 2023


Our main variable of interest was receiving an Appropriate and Timely Work-Up
defined as repeat PSA within 6 months and/or MRI or biopsy within 12 months
after the initial abnormal PSA test. Our primary endpoint was the occurrence of
Lethal PCa, defined as dying from PCa or being diagnosed with a metastatic
disease

Statistical analysis
• Cumulative incidence was used to depict Lethal PCa development stratified
  based on appropriate work-up status, and statistical significance was tested
  using Gray’s test.
• Competing-Risks Regressions analysis tested the impact of receiving an
  Appropriate Work-Up on Lethal Prostate Cancer risk .



 CONCLUSION
 Notably, nearly one in four patients does not receive timely and appropriate evaluation, highlighting a significant quality-of-care concern. Inadequate
 or delayed diagnostic work-up following an initial abnormal PSA result can negatively affect oncological outcomes in patients subsequently
 diagnosed with PCa when compared to their timely worked-up counterpart.

title: Prior 5-a-Reductase Inhibitor Exposure Associates with Enhanced ICI Benefit in Metastatic RCC: Multicentre Cohort with Single-Cell Immune Profiling
text:
IP78-17: Prior 5-a-Reductase Inhibitor Exposure Associates with Enhanced ICI Benefit in Metastatic
                     RCC: Multicentre Cohort with Single-Cell Immune Profiling
                                                            Cheng Bisheng, Peng Wu*
                              Department of Urology, Southern Medical University Nanfang Hospital, Guangzhou, China

                                                                              Methods
                                                                              Design, Setting, and Participants: Multicentre retrospective cohort of 185 mRCC
                                                                              patients receiving ICIs (2015–2020) at three tertiary hospitals. Patients were stratified
                                                                              by documented continuous 5-ARI use ≥12 months before ICI initiation; propensity
                                                                              score matching (PSM) balanced baseline covariates. A subset of fresh tumours
                                                                              underwent scRNA-seq. Intervention: ICIs alone or in standard combinations; prior
                                                                              finasteride/dutasteride exposure as the key variable of interest. Outcome
                                                                              Measurements and Statistical Analysis: Primary endpoints: progression-free survival
                                                                              (PFS) and overall survival (OS) by Kaplan–Meier and multivariable Cox models.
                                                                              Secondary endpoints: objective response rate (ORR), disease control rate (DCR), time
                                                                              to response, duration of response, and safety. Subgroup/sensitivity analyses were pre-
                                                                              specified; scRNA-seq profiled immune cell states and PD-1 expression.

                                                                              Results ＆ Conclusion
                                                                               Prior 5-ARI exposure associated with higher ORR (59.8% vs 39.8%, p=0.0075) and
                                                                              numerically higher DCR (87.0% vs 78.7%). Survival favoured the 5-ARI group (PFS
                                                                              HR 0.64, 95%CI 0.47–0.86, p=0.0085; OS HR 0.65, 95%CI 0.47–0.90, p=0.0271), with
                                                                              3-year OS 31.2% vs 15.0%. Responses occurred earlier (median TTR 2.8 vs 4.05
                                                                              months) and lasted longer (DoR 7.5 vs 1.8 months; both p<0.001). Grade ≥III adverse
Background ＆ Objective                                                        events were not increased. scRNA-seq showed reduced Tregs, lower CD8⁺ T-cell
                                                                              exhaustion and decreased PD-1 expression within exhausted CD8⁺ subsets among
Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) improve survival in metastatic renal      5-ARI-exposed patients, suggesting an immunologically favourable milieu. Benefits
cell carcinoma (mRCC), yet responses remain heterogeneous. Androgen-          were generally consistent across age, IMDC risk, PD-L1 status and metastatic
axis signalling can dampen CD8⁺ T-cell function; thus, prior exposure to 5-   burden.Pre-treatment exposure to 5-ARIs correlates with meaningfully improved ICI
α-reductase inhibitors (5-ARIs; finasteride/dutasteride) may favour ICI       effectiveness and favourable immune reprogramming in mRCC. These findings
efficacy by reshaping the tumour immune microenvironment.                     support prospective trials testing androgen-axis modulation as an inexpensive,
                                                                              scalable adjunct to immunotherapy and warrant evaluation of 5-ARI history as a readily
                                                                              available clinical stratifier.

title: THE MIAMI CANCER INSTITUTE TECHNIQUE: PUBOPROSTATIC LIGAMENT PRESERVATION WITH SELECTIVE DORSAL VENOUS COMPLEX LIGATION AND CYSTOURETHROPEXY
text:
Abstract 26-1337: THE MIAMI CANCER INSTITUTE TECHNIQUE:
                                                   PUBOPROSTATIC LIGAMENT PRESERVATION WITH SELECTIVE DORSAL
                                                   VENOUS COMPLEX LIGATION AND CYSTOURETHROPEXY

                                                   Authors: Deerush Kannan Sakthivel, Pushan Prabhakar, Mohamed Javid Raja Iyub,
                                                   Manuel Ozambela Jr, Murugesan Manoharan


INTRODUCTION
•Urinary incontinence after robot-assisted radical prostatectomy
(RARP) remains a major factor affecting postoperative quality of
life.
•Despite technical refinements, continence recovery continues to
be a challenge.
•The dorsal venous complex (DVC), traditionally considered a
venous structure, may contain neural elements important for
continence.
o Conventional early DVC ligation may compromise:
o External urethral sphincter
o Puboprostatic ligament (PPL)
o Injury to these structures may delay postoperative continence
    recovery.
•We describe a novel approach: Miami Cancer Institute (MCI)
Technique: It involves early selective DVC ligation with PPL
preservation followed by cystourethropexy
•This study evaluates the safety, oncological and continence
outcomes of this technique.

.



METHODS                                                            RESULTS
An analysis of 373 RARP patients (2017–2023) was conducted.        •   Mean age was 65.3 years. Operative time averaged 168.4 minutes; mean blood loss was 76.4 mL.
Exclusion criteria included prior pelvic surgery, radiation, or    •   No transfusions or Clavien III complications occurred.
preexisting incontinence.                                          •   Three-month continence was achieved in 83.1%. One-third later regained continence by 1 year.
The technique involved early DVC ligation with PPL preservation    •   Most had organ-confined, node-negative disease. Biochemical recurrence was 6.4% at 1 year, and 15% overall.
and cystourethropexy.                                              •   MCI technique showed favorable functional and oncological outcomes, even in a diverse cohort.
Primary outcome:
continence recovery at 3 months (defined as use of no pads or
one security pad per day).                                         CONCLUSIONS
Secondary outcomes included operative                              The MCI technique is a safe, effective, and reproducible approach in RARP.
time, blood loss, complications, and biochemical recurrence.       By preserving the PPL and combining cystourethropexy, it enhances early continence recovery without
Descriptive statistics and Kaplan-Meier estimates were used for    compromising oncologic control.
analysis.

INTRODUCTION                                                                                      RESULTS
Obesity presents significant technical and anatomical challenges during RARP,
restricting instrument mobility, obscuring surgical planes, and complicating
neurovascular bundle preservation, all of which may compromise the ability to achieve
clear surgical margins.

Positive surgical margins (PSMs) are associated with biochemical recurrence and the
need for adjuvant treatment. Whether obesity independently increases PSM risk
independent of tumour stage and grade remains poorly defined; this study addresses
that gap using a propensity score matched analysis from a prospective tertiary centre
registry.

title: Comparative Outcomes of Salvage Robotic Radical Prostatectomy After Radiation Therapy Versus Focal Therapy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
text:
26-6850: Comparative Outcomes of Salvage Robotic Radical
                                                                  Prostatectomy After Radiation Therapy Versus Focal Therapy:
                                                                  A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
                                                                  Andrade M.A., Baldissera-Cardoso R., Rodrigues H., Godinho N.J.S., Costa Rodrigues M.L.A., Gerspacher-Lara H.F., Bessa da Silva
                                                                  J.A., Andrade M.A., Donalisio da Silva R.




                                        PURPOSE
Recurrence of localized prostate cancer following primary non-surgical treatment, such as
radiotherapy (XRT) or focal therapy (FT), remains a clinical challenge. Salvage robotic-assisted
radical prostatectomy (sRARP) has emerged as a definitive option for selected patients with
localized recurrence. The impact of prior treatment modality on perioperative complexity,
functional recovery, and oncologic outcomes remains debated. This meta-analysis compares
sRARP outcomes after XRT versus FT.

                                        METHODS
PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane were searched through October 2025, following PRISMA
guidelines. Eligible studies compared sRARP outcomes in patients with recurrent localized
prostate cancer previously treated with XRT versus FT. Functional, perioperative, and oncologic
outcomes were extracted. Pooled analyses used random-effects models.



                                         RESULTS
Five studies including 791 patients (553 XRT, 238 FT) were analyzed, with median follow-up of
24–60 months for oncologic outcomes up to 5 years. sRARP after FT showed superior 12-month
urinary continence (0 pads) versus post-XRT (OR 0.29; 95% CI 0.16–0.52; p<0.0001; I²=58%),
with 3.4-fold higher odds. Erectile function at 12 months was also better post-FT (OR 0.29; 95%
CI 0.15–0.56; p=0.0006; I²=7%). Biochemical recurrence-free survival at 3–5 years was similar
(HR 1.22; 95% CI 0.95–1.57; p=0.12; I²=0%); one study reported worse overall survival post-XRT
(HR 5.1; p=0.02). Major complications (Clavien-Dindo ≥3) within 90 days were higher post-XRT
(OR 1.91; 95% CI 1.05–3.47; p=0.03). Operative time was comparable (MD -3.2 min; p=0.41).
Positive margins were higher post-FT (OR 2.15; 95% CI 1.23–3.76; p=0.007; I²=0%).


                                     CONCLUSION
Salvage robotic radical prostatectomy after focal therapy resulted in markedly superior functional
                                                                                                          Figure 1 - PRISMA flow diagram of study screening and selection.
outcomes versus post-radiation, with higher odds of complete urinary continence and erectile
function recovery at 12 months. Without biochemical recurrence-free survival benefit, prior
radiotherapy was linked to increased major perioperative complications. These findings indicate
that while oncologic efficacy is equivalent, sRARP following focal therapy offers significant
functional advantages and lower morbidity.

title: Development of a Preoperative Nomogram to Predict PSA Persistence After Robot-Assisted Radical Prostatectomy
text:
Development of a Preoperative Nomogram to Predict PSA Persistence
                            After Robot-Assisted Radical Prostatectomy        IP79-28
                                                              Yu Ozawa1, Marcio Covas Moschovas1, Marco Montesi1, Saleh Bubishate1,
                                                       Rohan Sharma1, Shady Saikali1, Marco Sandri2, Ari Diamond1, Travis Rogers1, Vipul Patel1
                                                                         1 AdventHealth Global Robotics Institute, Celebration, FL, USA

                                                                   2 Big and Open Data Innovation Laboratory (BODaI-Lab), Brescia, Italy


Introduction                                                Results
• PSA persistence after radical prostatectomy is a robust   • Based on NCCN criteria, 756 patients (18%) were classified as very low- to low-risk, 2,884 (69%) as
  predictor of adverse oncologic outcomes, yet no             intermediate-risk, and 572 (14%) as high- to very high-risk.
  preoperative tool is available to estimate its risk.      • A median preoperative PSA was 5.9 ng/mL (IQR 4.6–8.1). PSA persistence occurred in 4.0% (168/4,212).
• We aimed to develop a preoperative nomogram and
  clinical score predicting PSA persistence.
Methods
• This is a single-institutional retrospective study.
• We analyzed 4,212 men who underwent preoperative
  MRI and robot-assisted radical prostatectomy from
  August 2017 and February 2025.
• As a primary endpoint, PSA persistence was defined as
  a postoperative PSA that does not fall to undetectable
  levels (> 0.1 ng/mL) at 6–8 weeks after surgery.
                                                                                                            LASSO regression identified eight variables.
• We developed a nomogram and PSA persistence
  predictive (PPP) score, using clinicopathological and
  MRI variables.


                                                                                                                                                                            Model calibration was evaluated using 1,000 bootstrap resamples.
                                                                                                                                                                            The calibration curve demonstrated close agreement between
                                                                                                                                                                            predicted and observed probabilities (Supplementary Figure 3), with
                                                                                                                                                                            an optimism-corrected calibration slope of 0.96 and a calibration
                                                                                                                                                                            intercept of –0.10. The scaled Brier score was 0.11.




                                                                                               • The final model yielded an AUC of 0.79 (95% CI, 0.75–0.82)

                                                            PSA persistence predictive score
                                                            • We developed PPP score by rescaling each regression coefficient
                                                              relative to the coefficient for PPC ≥50% (β = 0.38 as reference).
                                                            • The median of PPP score was of 5 (IQR, 3–6; range 1–20).
                                                            • PPP score showed AUC of 0.79 (95% CI, 0.75–0.82), preserved
                                                              calibration (1.0006; intercept 0.0042), and a scaled Brier score of
                                                              0.106, which is comparable to the full multivariable model.

                                                            Conclusion
                                                            • We developed the first preoperative nomogram and clinical score predicting PSA persistence following robot-assisted radical prostatectomy.
                                                            • The main limitation is surgical selection bias. External prospective validation is warranted to determine the generalizability of these findings.

title: Maintaining Quality of Life during Survivorship for Patients diagnosed with Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: The use of the electronic Cancer Resource, Information, and Support (CRIS) Platform
text:
11/3/25, 10:41 AM                                                           AUA2026 Submission Site

    26-6864
    Maintaining Quality of Life during Survivorship for Patients diagnosed with Muscle Invasive
    Bladder Cancer: The use of the electronic Cancer Resource, Information, and Support
    (CRIS) Platform
    Michael A Diefenbach1, Simon J Hall1, Alexander Kutikov2, Manish Vira1, Allison Marziliano1, Stephani Groton1, Suzanne M Miller2
    1
      Northwell Health, New Hyde Park, NY, 2Fox Chase Cancer Center, Philadelphia, PA
    INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES:

    Muscle invasive bladder cancer (MIBC), treated surgically with cystectomy, affects both patients
    and caregivers, who experience significant practical challenges and declining quality of life (QOL).
    To prevent declines in QOL and address survivor challenges we evaluated our newly developed
    Cancer Resource and Information Support (CRIS) software (versus enhanced Standard of Care;
    eSOC) in a randomized controlled trial, conducted among two large health care systems in the
    northeast of the US.


    METHODS:

    Patients diagnosed with MIBC (n = 109) and their caregivers (n = 65) were randomized after
    treatment to receive CRIS or eSOC. CRIS is an interactive comprehensive software program for
    patients and caregivers consisting of MIBC-relevant videos by providers, survivor and caregiver
    testimonials, text and graphics, to provide instrumental and psychosocial support, particularly
    during the earliest period of survivorship. eSOC consisted of the NCI publication Facing Forward:
    Life after Cancer Treatment. Facing Forward is non-specific to MIBC, addressing all cancer
    survivors. Assessments were completed at Baseline (after treatment) and at 1,3,6, and 12 months
    post baseline. The primary outcomes were bladder cancer specific QOL (FACT-BL-CYS) for
    patients and the Caregiver QOL Index-C (CQOLC) for caregivers.


    RESULTS:

    At 1-month post baseline patients in the CRIS group reported an unchanged level of QOL (M=0.50;
    ±21.11) whereas patients in the eSOC group reported a M= 9.66 (±22.03) point decline, a
    statistically and clinically significant difference in QOL. QOL increased over time for both groups,
    but remained higher for patients randomized to CRIS over the 12-month follow-up. Results were
    not duplicated among Caregivers. Those in the CRIS group reported a statistically significant but
    not clinically meaningful decline in QOL M = -3.80 (±7.14), whereas patients in the eSOC group’s
    QOL improved slightly M= 0.76 (±6.95). Over time, caregiver QOL increased in both groups to
    reach similar levels. There were no demographic moderator effects between study arms.


    CONCLUSIONS:

    CRIS provided instrumental and psychosocial support for patients, preventing a clinically
    meaningful decline in QOL after treatment compared to patients randomized into eSOC.
    Caregivers, compared to patients, reacted differently to CRIS. Caregiver content in CRIS was more
    realistic compared to the positive information in Facing Forward. This might have influenced
    caregivers’ QOL ratings. The significant QOL results among patients deserve further evaluation
    within different clinical and practice settings among varied populations.


    SOURCE OF FUNDING: 1R01CA224918-01A (NCI) to Diefenbach & Miller

title: Strategic Integration of Advanced Practice Providers (APPs) in a Tertiary Referral Urologic Oncology Center: A Three-Year Health Services Evaluation
text:
26-9321: Strategic Integration of Advanced Practice Providers (APPs) in a
                                                                        Tertiary Referral Urologic Oncology Center: A Three-Year Health Services
                                                                        Evaluation
                                                                        Jewel Bamby, Divya Kurup, Darren Deoraj, Ketan Badani
                                                                        Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY




Introduction                                                                Results
As patient complexity escalates and urology faces workforce
constraints, advanced practice providers (APPs) have emerged
as critical contributors to care delivery. However, their integration
often remains reactive and underutilized, limiting clinical impact.
This study evaluates the impact of a structured APP integration
model on access, throughput, and provider efficiency within a
tertiary referral urologic oncology program.


Methods
Retrospective review of departmental operations at Mount Sinai
Health System (January 2022 – June 2024)

Mid-2022 intervention redefined APP roles to:
 – Independently manage survivorship & surveillance visits
 – Perform routine procedures
 – Co-manage new consults

Monthly charges, payments, and APP-only revenue analyzed to
assess:
  – Service volume
  – Inpatient–outpatient distribution
  – Operational performance

Provider surveys captured perceptions of workflow efficiency and
satisfaction (analysis ongoing)

Funding

None

Peyronie’s disease (PD) is a fibrotic disorder of the
tunica albuginea of the penis that may cause deformity
with a significant impact on patients’ quality of life. The
chronic phase of PD surgical treatment can be offered,
depending on the degree of curvature and the
complexity of the deformity. For complex deformities,
plaque incision and grafting is a good option.
The objective is to compare surgical outcomes between
polyglycolic acid Polymer grafts and porcine small
intestinal submucosa (SIS) grafts in patients undergoing
plaque incision and grafting for PD.

    INTRODUCTION                                                                                                     RESULTS
     Pathological complete response (CR, ypT0N0) at radical cystectomy (RC) strongly
     predicts survival in bladder cancer. While extensively studied after neoadjuvant
     therapy, predictors of CR following upfront RC remain poorly defined. We aimed to
     identify TURBT- and patient-derived factors associated with CR and to develop a                                                centrally reviewed and
     nomogram predicting individual response probabilities.                                                                         graded using PI-QUAL
MATERIALS & METHODS                                                                                                                 v2 and PI-RADS v2.1


                                        We retrospectively reviewed 1,054 patients who
                                        underwent RC at a tertiary center between 2012 and
                                        2025, without neoadjuvant therapy and with a
                                        documented complete TURBT prior to surgery                                                      Multifoc
                                                                                                                                        ality


• Due to limited sample size and low CR frequency, a synthetic cohort
  from the baseline dataset of 1,054 patients was generated using the
  synthpop R package.
• Multivariable logistic regression identified predictors of CR, which were
  used to construct a nomogram.
• Model performance was assessed by discrimination (AUC) and
  calibration, with internal validation via leave-one-out cross-validation
                                                                                                                      Among 136 patients19 (14%) achieved CR. TURBT stage distribution was 60% T2, 15% T1, and 20% Ta/Tis.
  (LOOCV) and external validation on the original dataset.                                                           In the expanded dataset (n = 1,000; CR 15%), tumor size >3 cm (OR 0.44, p = 0.019), multifocality (OR 0.62,
                                                                                                                       p = 0.020), trigone/peri-ostial (OR 0.40, p = 0.004) or anterior/neck location (OR 0.27, p = 0.028), and CIS
                                                                                                                      (OR 0.43, p = 0.001) independently predicted lower odds of CR. The nomogram showed good calibration
                                                                                                                          (intercept = 0, slope = 1, Emax = 0.60, Eavg = 0.010) and acceptable discrimination (AUC = 0.70). In
                                                                                                                                             LOOCV, AUC = 0.65; applied to the original dataset, AUC = 0.74
    CONCLUSION
    This exploratory analysis identifies TURBT and tumor features predictive of pathological CR after upfront RC and provides the first nomogram to
    estimate individualized response probability in patients not receiving neoadjuvant therapy. External validation in larger, multicenter datasets is
    warranted to confirm its clinical utility for patient counseling and trial design.

METHODS
Using the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and
End Results database (2004–2022),
pT2N0M0 urothelial bladder cancer patients
treated with TMT were identified.
Sequential testing of tumor size cutoffs of 3,
4, 5, 6, and 7 cm were applied.
Propensity score matching and multivariable
competing risks regression (CRR) models
were used.



CONCLUSIONS
Tumor size is directly proportional to CSM rate in pT2N0M0 urothelial bladder cancer treated with TMT.

Applying established and recommended non-inferiority margins in oncology trials of up to 30% suggests that tumor size cutoff of 6 cm (HR 1.72)
could represent a clinically meaningful criterion used in patient selection for TMT.

title: Spatial transcriptomic profiling of TSC-associated angiomyolipoma reveals molecular heterogeneity distinct from sporadic AML
text:
Spatial transcriptomic profiling of TSC-associated angiomyolipoma reveals
                                                                                                                             molecular heterogeneity distinct from sporadic AML
       IP84-02                                                                                                   Ryuta Watanabe1*, Kensuke Shishiso, Shota Nobumori, Naoya Sugihara, Keigo Nishida, Haruna Arai, Takatora Sawada,
                                                                                                                        Shunsuke Haga, Osuke Arai, Tomoya Onishi, Kenichi Nishimura1, Tetsuya Fukumoto1, Noriyoshi Miura1,
                                                                                                                                Mie Kurata2,3, Riko Kitazawa4, Yuki Miyauchi, Tadahiko Kikugawa 1, Takashi Saika1
                                                                                                                      1 Department of Urology, Ehime University Hospital, 2 Department of Analytical Pathology, Ehime University Graduate School of Medicine
                                                                                                                   3 Department of Pathology, Ehime University Proteo-Science Center 4 Division of Diagnostic Pathology, Ehime University Hospital, Toon, Japan

                                            Background                                                                                                                                                                               Results
⚫   Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC): autosomal-
    dominant disorder caused by TSC1/TSC2 loss →
    chronic mTORC1 hyperactivation
⚫   Renal angiomyolipoma (AML): common in TSC
    (≈80%); triphasic tumor with vascular, smooth
    muscle, and adipose components
    ✓ TSC-associated AML (TSC-AML) differs from
        sporadic AML:Often bilateral, multifocal, and
        larger
                                                           Marafie et al., Int. J. Mol. Sci. 2024
    ✓ May show aggressive, epithelioid features             TSC-associated angiomyolipoma is driven by constitutive mTORC1
    ✓ Responds to mTOR inhibitors (e.g.,                    activation due to loss of TSC1/TSC2.
        everolimus) but regrows after discontinuation

⚫  A better understanding of its underlying pathogenesis
   may enable the development of curative therapies for
   TSC-associated angiomyolipoma.
⚫ Spatial transcriptomics preserves tissue architecture                                              Crino et al. N Engl J Med. 2006

→ ideal for analyzing triphasic tumors
                                                                            TSC1/TSC2-deficient cells undergo multilineage
                                                                            differentiation to form angiomyolipoma.



                                             Objective
⚫   To elucidate the molecular landscape and microenvironmental differences between: TSC-AML,
    Sporadic AML, Renal cell carcinoma (RCC)
⚫   To identify TSC-specific transcriptional signatures using spatial transcriptomics

                                                                                                                                       Limitation
                                               Methods                                                                                 • Small sample size (one case per tumor type); exploratory analysis
                                                                                                                                       • FFPE tissue with 55-µm spot resolution, not true single-cell resolution
                                                                                                                                       • Transcriptomic analysis only; mTORC1 activity (phosphorylation) was not directly assessed
                                        ⚫   Spatial transcriptomics: CytAssist Visium (10x Genomics) on                                • No functional validation and no external cohort validation
                                            FFPE samples
                                        ⚫   Cases: one each of TSC-AML, sporadic AML, and RCC

title: Pathological Characteristics and Clinical Features of the Borderline Region in Renal Cell Carcinoma: Exploring Mechanisms of Tumor Invasion and Metastasis
text:
Pathological Characteristics and Clinical Features of the Borderline
                                                                   Region in Renal Cell Carcinoma: Exploring Mechanisms of Tumor
                                                                   Invasion and Metastasis
                                                                   Peizhe Li1, Huiying He2, Min Lu2, Ye Yan1, Jianfei Ye1, Fan Zhang1, Hongxian Zhang1, Chuxiao Xu1,
                                                                   Ruiyang Xie1, Yimeng Song1, Shuhua Wei3, Shudong Zhang1#, Lulin Ma1#
                                                                   1. Dept. of Urology Surgery, PUTH, Beijing   2. Dept. of Pathology, School of Basic Med. Sci., PUTH & PKUHSC, Beijing   3. Dept. of Radiation Oncology, PUTH, Beijing




【Objective】
Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is a common urological malignancy. This study aims to investigate the pathological characteristics and
associated clinical features of the tumor-stroma interface (border zone) of RCC. By analyzing the cellular composition, molecular
features, and microenvironmental changes in the border zone, we seek to uncover the potential mechanisms underlying RCC invasion
and metastasis, and to provide a scientific basis for future comprehensive treatment strategies.

【Methods】
Standardized special sampling techniques were used to precisely obtain specimens from the border zone between RCC tumor and
normal tissue. HE staining, immunohistochemistry, and other techniques were employed to systematically evaluate cell morphology,
immune cell infiltration patterns, and expression of key proteins in this region. Meanwhile, using a digital pathology platform, whole
slide images (WSIs) of the border zone were extracted. A multiple instance learning (MIL) framework combined with explainable
artificial intelligence (XAI) methods was applied to perform in-depth modeling and analysis of image features, thereby improving the
accuracy and interpretability of pathological recognition. Clinical data of patients were integrated to construct correlation analysis
models, exploring the relationship between border zone characteristics and patient survival outcomes.

【Results】
This study successfully identified and quantified several key histopathological features in the RCC border zone, including tumor
budding, desmoplastic reaction, and immune cell infiltration patterns. Further analysis revealed significant immunosuppression and
metabolic dysregulation in this region, along with specific upregulation of pro-inflammatory and immune escape-related genes in
certain cell subsets surrounding the tumor. These pathological and molecular abnormalities were closely associated with tumor
invasiveness and metastatic potential. Clinical data further confirmed that specific morphological features of the border zone were
significantly correlated with patient prognosis; patients with highly aggressive features showed worse overall survival and higher risk
of recurrence.

【Conclusion】
This study is the first to systematically delineate the pathological characteristics of the RCC border zone, highlighting its critical role in
tumor invasion and metastasis. Specific molecular and cellular changes within the border zone may serve as important biomarkers for
predicting prognosis in RCC patients, and also offer potential therapeutic targets for the development of novel targeted treatment
strategies, thereby providing new research directions and practical pathways for advancing precision therapy in renal cell carcinoma.
